Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Vulnerable Pterodactyl Wings node (< v1.12.3) exposed to CVE-2026-52855 config-secret disclosure
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Pterodactyl Wings daemon-token file (/etc/pterodactyl/config.yml) read by non-Wings process
Vulnerable Pterodactyl Wings node (< v1.12.3) exposed to CVE-2026-52855 config-secret disclosure AIExploitation High
Surfaces hosts running Pterodactyl Wings below v1.12.3, which exposes the full daemon config (including the node daemon token, token_id and docker.registries credentials) to egg configuration-file templating. A low-privileged server owner can smuggle a {{config.token}} placeholder and read the node's daemon token, enabling full-node compromise. This is asset-exposure triage, not a behavioural signature. Rationale: Keys on the article's two concrete disclosure values: the fixed version boundary v1.12.3 and CVE-2026-52855 for the go package github.com/pterodactyl/wings. Confirmed the node token / token_id / docker.registries live in config.yml via pkg.go.dev and the Wings config docs. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-pfvc-3p5h-x7h6 • https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/pterodactyl/wings/config • https://pterodactyl-wings.mintlify.app/configuration/config-file
ATT&CKT1190 T1552.001
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Decommissioned/offline nodes still present in stale software inventory
  • Isolated single-tenant nodes where no untrusted user can set egg variables (still vulnerable but lower real risk)
  • Nodes already patched to 1.12.3+ but scanner data not yet refreshed
  • Lab/staging Wings instances intentionally kept on old versions
  • Custom-forked wings builds whose version string does not follow semver and mis-parses
Suppression filter
| where OSPlatform in~ ("Linux")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the Wings version on the node (`wings --version`) and whether it is multi-tenant / shared-hosting (untrusted users can set egg variables) — those are the exposed ones. 2) Contain: upgrade Wings to v1.12.3+, then per the advisory rotate the node daemon token (Admin -> Nodes -> Configuration -> reset token) and re-deploy config.yml, since a previously exfiltrated token stays valid until rotated. 3) Hunt: review the node's server volumes and SFTP/file-manager access logs for prior reads of rendered config files, and pivot to UC-2 for any process that touched /etc/pterodactyl/config.yml.
DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where SoftwareName has "wings" and (SoftwareVendor has "pterodactyl" or SoftwareName has "pterodactyl")
| extend ParsedVer = parse_version(SoftwareVersion)
| where ParsedVer < parse_version("1.12.3")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, OSPlatform
| order by DeviceName asc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId == "CVE-2026-52855" or (SoftwareName has "wings" and SoftwareVendor has "pterodactyl")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by DeviceName asc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Vulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities where Vulnerabilities.cve="CVE-2026-52855" OR (Vulnerabilities.signature="*wings*" AND Vulnerabilities.signature="*pterodactyl*") by Vulnerabilities.dest Vulnerabilities.signature Vulnerabilities.severity Vulnerabilities.cve | `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)` | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Vulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities where Vulnerabilities.cve="CVE-2026-52855" OR (Vulnerabilities.signature="*wings*" AND Vulnerabilities.signature="*pterodactyl*") by Vulnerabilities.dest Vulnerabilities.signature Vulnerabilities.severity Vulnerabilities.cve | `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)` | sort - lastTime
Pterodactyl Wings daemon-token file (/etc/pterodactyl/config.yml) read by non-Wings process AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts hands-on-keyboard theft of the exact secrets CVE-2026-52855 discloses — the daemon token, token_id and docker.registries stored in /etc/pterodactyl/config.yml. Any process other than the wings daemon that cats, copies, greps or archives this file is high-signal for credential theft on a compromised node. Companion to the version-exposure UC; the templating exfil itself is content-only and not visible in host telemetry. Rationale: Uses the article's concrete secret store: /etc/pterodactyl/config.yml holds config.token (daemon token + JWT HMAC key), config.token_id and config.docker.registries. Confirmed this exact path via the Wings config docs and pkg.go.dev config package. Excludes the legitimate wings daemon to isolate theft. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-pfvc-3p5h-x7h6 • https://pterodactyl-wings.mintlify.app/configuration/config-file • https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/pterodactyl/wings/config
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1078
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Operator manually inspecting config.yml during maintenance (cat/less/vim)
  • Backup or archival jobs (tar/rsync/cp of /etc/pterodactyl) sweeping the config
  • Configuration-management runs (Ansible/Puppet/Chef) templating or reading config.yml
  • Monitoring/inventory agents fingerprinting installed software
  • Wings upgrade/reinstall scripts copying the config to a backup before rewrite
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("tar","rsync","ansible","puppet","chef-client","salt-minion","cp") and FileName !in~ ("tar","rsync")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the reading process, user, and parent — was it an interactive shell (attacker) or a known backup/config-mgmt daemon? Check the account against expected node admins. 2) Contain: if unexpected, isolate the node, rotate the daemon token (Admin -> Nodes -> reset token, re-deploy config.yml) and any docker registry credentials it referenced, and revoke active Wings JWTs. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host/user for other server volumes accessed, SFTP downloads of rendered config files, and outbound use of the token against the Panel<->Wings API on other servers of that node.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has @"/etc/pterodactyl/config.yml"
| where FileName !in~ ("wings")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "/etc/pterodactyl/config.yml"
| where ActingProcessName !endswith "/wings" and ActingProcessName !~ "wings"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-52855")

| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).

Malicious 'anthropickit' PyPI package installed via pip (supply-chain cred stealer) AIInstallation High
Hunts pip/python installing the specific malicious package 'anthropickit' whose setup.py steals SSH keys and CI secrets at install time. Targets the exact package name (dependency-confusion sentinel v999.9.9) rather than a generic pip-install template. Rationale: Anchors on the exact package name 'anthropickit' (confirmed by OSV MAL-2026-904 and CIRCL MAL-2026-5755) combined with a pip/python execution context; the name is unique enough that any hit is the malicious package, not a false positive. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/anthropic-rogue-agents-package-stole-keys • https://osv.dev/vulnerability/MAL-2026-904 • https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/mal-2026-5755 • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/anthropic-says-claude-mistook-open.html
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1204.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer intentionally testing/reverse-engineering the malware sample in a sandbox
  • Security-vendor package scanners that install-and-detonate PyPI packages (this is exactly how one victim in the article was hit — treat as TP unless known scanner infra)
  • Internal wiki/ticket automation echoing the package name into a shell command that never actually installs it
  • A benign internal package deliberately named 'anthropickit' (none known to exist)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "sandbox" and DeviceName !in~ ("malware-analysis-01","pkg-scanner-01")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host actually ran 'pip install anthropickit' vs. merely referencing the string; pull the full process tree and the invoking user/CI job. 2) Contain: kill the CI runner / isolate the host, rotate ALL SSH private keys under the affected identity and every env-var secret matching KEY/SECRET/TOKEN/PASS/AUTH/API, and revoke associated cloud/API tokens — assume full compromise the instant install ran. 3) Hunt: search the fleet for /tmp/runner_exfil.json and outbound connections to pipedream.net from the same hosts (see companion UCs); pivot on the same PyPI account/mirror config to find other pulled packages.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "anthropickit" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "anthropickit"
| where FileName has_any ("pip","pip3","python","python3") or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("pip install","setup.py","-m pip")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "anthropickit"
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("pip","python") or TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("pip install","setup.py","-m pip")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

anthropickit loot file '/tmp/runner_exfil.json' written to disk AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts creation of the exact loot file the anthropickit stealer writes before exfiltration, containing harvested SSH keys and CI secrets. Near-zero-FP file artifact unique to this malware ('runner_exfil.json' in /tmp). Rationale: The filename 'runner_exfil.json' in /tmp is a hardcoded, unique artifact of this specific stealer (verified in the setup.py sample and CIRCL/OSV writeups); its presence is effectively pathognomonic and needs no threshold. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/anthropic-rogue-agents-package-stole-keys • https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/mal-2026-5755 • https://osv.dev/vulnerability/MAL-2026-904
ATT&CKT1005 T1074.001 T1552.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analysts detonating the sample in a lab (file will legitimately appear)
  • An IR/forensics playbook that copies the recovered loot file back to /tmp on a test box
  • A coincidentally-named internal script writing runner_exfil.json (no legitimate tool is known to use this name)
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture and hash the file, note the writing process (should be python/pip); the JSON contents reveal exactly which SSH keys and env secrets were harvested. 2) Contain: isolate the host/runner and immediately rotate every credential enumerated in the file plus all SSH private keys for the identity; delete the file only after evidence capture. 3) Hunt: correlate with 'pip install anthropickit' execution and outbound pipedream.net traffic on the same host; sweep all CI runners sharing the same base image or secret store.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FileName =~ "runner_exfil.json" or FolderPath has "/tmp/runner_exfil.json"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "runner_exfil.json" or TargetFilePath has "runner_exfil.json"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

anthropickit exfiltration POST to Pipedream endpoint (enqqnvvtgrnyl.x.pipedream.net) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the outbound exfiltration channel used by anthropickit — a python/pip process reaching a Pipedream webhook to POST stolen SSH keys and CI secrets. Anchors on the specific IOC host and the broader python→pipedream.net pattern. Rationale: Uses the exact hardcoded exfil host enqqnvvtgrnyl.x.pipedream.net (high-fidelity IOC in Sigma) plus the durable python/pip→pipedream.net pattern for endpoints where the specific throwaway URL has rotated; process context suppresses benign developer Pipedream use. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/anthropic-rogue-agents-package-stole-keys • https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/mal-2026-5755 • https://osv.dev/vulnerability/MAL-2026-904 • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/anthropics-claude-breached-3-orgs-uploaded-pypi-malware-during-tests/
ATT&CKT1567 T1041 T1552.001
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers legitimately using Pipedream workflow webhooks from python scripts (broad pipedream.net clause — the exact IOC host clause has no legit use)
  • Python-based monitoring/CI integrations that POST to pipedream.net endpoints
  • A requests-based app whose parent is python but is unrelated to the stealer
  • Package scanners detonating the sample and generating the beacon
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteUrl has "pipedream.net" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("webhook","scheduled-job") and DeviceName in~ ("ci-integration-01"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the destination is the exact IOC host (definitive TP) or generic pipedream.net (verify against a known-good Pipedream allowlist); pull the initiating process and command line. 2) Contain: block pipedream.net at egress for CI/build ranges, isolate the host, and rotate all SSH keys and secrets — the POST body is the exfiltrated credential set. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for 'pip install anthropickit' and /tmp/runner_exfil.json; review the PyPI/mirror config to identify what else was pulled and which secrets store the runner could reach.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "pipedream.net" or RemoteUrl has "enqqnvvtgrnyl"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python","python3","pip","pip3") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("setup.py","pip install")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has "pipedream.net"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName, DstIpAddr
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("4ae13303fa1663a36cfaa70bebe77b52b12dbf17eef24db15c6c24c631d38fbf", "f3e103a8a230b5fb3066fb0a9eb7f5fdf5831d4c7b71a9d83de54d8d6673eae2", "ff4126bd465ae6de09a2eaa94a4fd2d7d385a5dae2c093372668d4b7ecb81633", "584ef638a5415f4eccf6645abbcd06198e9abecf8b75cbd9328aa58962d9b38b", "7df12487bade710459ccea2d3570cdbc") or SHA1 in~ ("4ae13303fa1663a36cfaa70bebe77b52b12dbf17eef24db15c6c24c631d38fbf", "f3e103a8a230b5fb3066fb0a9eb7f5fdf5831d4c7b71a9d83de54d8d6673eae2", "ff4126bd465ae6de09a2eaa94a4fd2d7d385a5dae2c093372668d4b7ecb81633", "584ef638a5415f4eccf6645abbcd06198e9abecf8b75cbd9328aa58962d9b38b", "7df12487bade710459ccea2d3570cdbc") or MD5 in~ ("4ae13303fa1663a36cfaa70bebe77b52b12dbf17eef24db15c6c24c631d38fbf", "f3e103a8a230b5fb3066fb0a9eb7f5fdf5831d4c7b71a9d83de54d8d6673eae2", "ff4126bd465ae6de09a2eaa94a4fd2d7d385a5dae2c093372668d4b7ecb81633", "584ef638a5415f4eccf6645abbcd06198e9abecf8b75cbd9328aa58962d9b38b", "7df12487bade710459ccea2d3570cdbc")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("4ae13303fa1663a36cfaa70bebe77b52b12dbf17eef24db15c6c24c631d38fbf", "f3e103a8a230b5fb3066fb0a9eb7f5fdf5831d4c7b71a9d83de54d8d6673eae2", "ff4126bd465ae6de09a2eaa94a4fd2d7d385a5dae2c093372668d4b7ecb81633", "584ef638a5415f4eccf6645abbcd06198e9abecf8b75cbd9328aa58962d9b38b", "7df12487bade710459ccea2d3570cdbc") or SHA1 in~ ("4ae13303fa1663a36cfaa70bebe77b52b12dbf17eef24db15c6c24c631d38fbf", "f3e103a8a230b5fb3066fb0a9eb7f5fdf5831d4c7b71a9d83de54d8d6673eae2", "ff4126bd465ae6de09a2eaa94a4fd2d7d385a5dae2c093372668d4b7ecb81633", "584ef638a5415f4eccf6645abbcd06198e9abecf8b75cbd9328aa58962d9b38b", "7df12487bade710459ccea2d3570cdbc") or MD5 in~ ("4ae13303fa1663a36cfaa70bebe77b52b12dbf17eef24db15c6c24c631d38fbf", "f3e103a8a230b5fb3066fb0a9eb7f5fdf5831d4c7b71a9d83de54d8d6673eae2", "ff4126bd465ae6de09a2eaa94a4fd2d7d385a5dae2c093372668d4b7ecb81633", "584ef638a5415f4eccf6645abbcd06198e9abecf8b75cbd9328aa58962d9b38b", "7df12487bade710459ccea2d3570cdbc")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["4ae13303fa1663a36cfaa70bebe77b52b12dbf17eef24db15c6c24c631d38fbf", "f3e103a8a230b5fb3066fb0a9eb7f5fdf5831d4c7b71a9d83de54d8d6673eae2", "ff4126bd465ae6de09a2eaa94a4fd2d7d385a5dae2c093372668d4b7ecb81633", "584ef638a5415f4eccf6645abbcd06198e9abecf8b75cbd9328aa58962d9b38b", "7df12487bade710459ccea2d3570cdbc"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Cheap Android TV Boxes Pose as Phones and Turn Owners’ Broadband Into Proxies

The Hacker News
2026-07-31 8 use cases 4 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

Bitsight says some cheap Android TV boxes have shipped with apps that rewrite their hardware identity to mimic Samsung, Huawei, Xiaomi, or Vivo phones, then click ads on websites run by the same operators. Researchers named the operation Fuyao and attributed it to Zhejiang Fengwo IoT Technology Co., Ltd., a mainland China company founded in 2019. The same apps have a second job. When a box

Actions on Objectives
Likely
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Fuyao Android TV-box botnet C2/backdoor egress to fwgcloud.com · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Fuyao Android TV-box botnet C2/backdoor egress to fwgcloud.com AICommand & Control Medium
Surfaces any host or on-network device resolving or connecting to fwgcloud.com, the expired-then-sinkholed domain Bitsight identified as the Fuyao operation's factory backdoor and telemetry collector. Article-specific because it anchors on the single confirmed network indicator tied to the Zhejiang Fengwo 'Fuyao' Android-TV-box ad-fraud / SOCKS5 residential-proxy botnet, not generic beaconing. Rationale: Anchors on fwgcloud.com — the single confirmed Fuyao network indicator, which Bitsight uncovered by registering the expired domain and using it as a sinkhole/factory-backdoor collector. Any enterprise host or managed device resolving it indicates a Fuyao-infected TV box or a related implant on the network. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/cheap-android-tv-boxes-pose-as-phones.html • https://www.bitsight.com/blog
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1090.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security-tooling / sinkhole or threat-intel appliance deliberately resolving fwgcloud.com for enrichment
  • A researcher or analyst manually browsing to the domain during triage
  • Passive-DNS or DNS-logging collectors replaying historical queries into the SIEM
  • Typo-squat or unrelated benign subdomain that happens to end in the same string (low likelihood given full-domain anchor)
Suppression filter
| where Computer !in~ ("sinkhole-collector01", "ti-enrichment01") and ClientProc !in~ ("threatintel.exe", "dnscollector.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the resolving/connecting asset via DeviceName/ClientIP; determine whether it is a managed endpoint or an unmanaged IoT/Android device on guest/corporate VLAN. Correlate the initiating process and any HDMI-linked network segment. Step 2 (contain): Sinkhole/block fwgcloud.com at DNS and egress firewall; quarantine or network-isolate the offending device (per FBI June-2025 guidance, disconnect suspect streaming boxes). Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the source IP for SOCKS5-style outbound relaying, ad-domain callbacks to any of Bitsight's 144 operator domains, S3 fetches of JavaScript fraud modules, and spoofed device-identifier (Samsung/Huawei/Xiaomi/Vivo) beacons from the same NAT/segment.
let c2domain = "fwgcloud.com";
union isfuzzy=true
  (DeviceNetworkEvents
   | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
   | where RemoteUrl has c2domain
   | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ClientProc = InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, SrcTable = "DeviceNetworkEvents"),
  (DeviceEvents
   | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
   | where ActionType == "DnsQueryResponse"
   | where AdditionalFields has c2domain or RemoteUrl has c2domain
   | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ClientProc = InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort = int(null), SrcTable = "DeviceEvents-DNS")
| order by Timestamp desc
let c2domain = "fwgcloud.com";
union isfuzzy=true
  (DnsEvents
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where Name has c2domain
   | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Domain = Name, SrcTable = "DnsEvents"),
  (ImDnsActivity
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where DnsQuery has c2domain
   | project TimeGenerated, Computer = DvcHostname, ClientIP = SrcIpAddr, Domain = DnsQuery, SrcTable = "ImDnsActivity"),
  (CommonSecurityLog
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where DestinationHostName has c2domain or RequestURL has c2domain or DestinationDnsDomain has c2domain
   | project TimeGenerated, Computer = SourceHostName, ClientIP = SourceIP, Domain = coalesce(DestinationHostName, DestinationDnsDomain, RequestURL), SrcTable = "CommonSecurityLog")
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Fuyao Android TV-Box Botnet C2/Backdoor Domain Resolution (fwgcloud.com)
id: 8f2c1e4a-6b7d-4c93-9a1f-2d5e0c7b4a11
description: Detects DNS resolution of fwgcloud.com, the factory-backdoor and telemetry-collector domain tied to the Zhejiang Fengwo Fuyao Android TV-box ad-fraud / SOCKS5 residential-proxy botnet (Bitsight).
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/cheap-android-tv-boxes-pose-as-phones.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/31
tags:
  - attack.command_and_control
  - attack.t1071.001
  - attack.t1090.002
logsource:
  category: dns
detection:
  selection:
    query|endswith: 'fwgcloud.com'
  condition: selection
level: high
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/(^|\.)fwgcloud\.com$/i | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, DomainName], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(DNS.record_type) as record_type from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS where DNS.query="*fwgcloud.com" by DNS.src DNS.query DNS.dest index sourcetype | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)` | append [| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where (All_Traffic.dest="*fwgcloud.com" OR All_Traffic.url="*fwgcloud.com") by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.app | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`] | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(DNS.record_type) as record_type from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS where DNS.query="*fwgcloud.com" by DNS.src DNS.query DNS.dest index sourcetype | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)` | append [| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where (All_Traffic.dest="*fwgcloud.com" OR All_Traffic.url="*fwgcloud.com") by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.app | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`] | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("") or RemoteUrl has_any ("fwgcloud.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let BadIPs     = dynamic([""]);
let BadDomains = dynamic(["fwgcloud.com"]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr in (BadIPs)
   or Url has_any (BadDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time

| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Critical

6 Reasons Why Device Code Phishing is the Fastest-Growing Threat of 2026

The Hacker News
2026-07-31 8 use cases 5 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

Device code phishing - the abuse of the OAuth 2.0 device authorization grant to steal access tokens - has evolved from a niche red-team technique to an industrial-scale threat in under six months. Designed for input-constrained devices like smart TVs, printers, and so on, the device authorization login flow has been adopted by a wide range of apps and use-cases that it wasn't originally

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Device code phishing token redemption via Microsoft Authentication Broker sign-in · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] ARToken post-token abuse: inbox rules & SharePoint exfil from device-code sign-in IP · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Device code phishing token redemption via Microsoft Authentication Broker sign-in AIExploitation Medium
Hunts successful Entra sign-ins through the Microsoft Authentication Broker app (AppId 29d9ed98-a469-4536-ade2-f981bc1d605e) against Device Registration Service / Microsoft Graph — the redemption footprint of an OAuth device authorization grant token captured by device code phishing kits (Storm-2372, EvilTokens/ARToken, DEBULL). This is the only server-side artifact of a device code phish since the victim interacts with legitimate Microsoft URLs. Rationale: Pivots on the concrete Microsoft Authentication Broker AppId (29d9ed98-a469-4536-ade2-f981bc1d605e) + Device Registration Service resource, the redemption footprint documented across Storm-2372 (Microsoft) and DEBULL (ZeroBEC) — the only reliable server-side artifact given the article's point that the flow transits legitimate Microsoft URLs. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/02/13/storm-2372-conducts-device-code-phishing-campaign/ • https://zerobec.com/blog/debull-storm-2372-microsoft-device-code-phishing-graphspy • https://www.wiz.io/blog/recent-oauth-attacks-detection-strategies
ATT&CKT1528 T1566.002
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Intune/Autopilot device enrollment which also transacts through the Microsoft Authentication Broker
  • Developers authenticating CLI tools or WAM broker on new corporate laptops
  • Windows Hello for Business provisioning against Device Registration Service
  • BYOD workplace-join of a personal device by a genuine employee
  • Conditional Access-driven re-registration after a device reset
Suppression filter
// Suppress users who routinely redeem via the broker (baseline) — leftanti against 30d history
let Baseline = SigninLogs | where TimeGenerated between (ago(30d) .. ago(2d)) | where AppId == "29d9ed98-a469-4536-ade2-f981bc1d605e" | summarize by UserPrincipalName; // join kind=leftanti on UserPrincipalName to surface first-time redeemers only
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: For each hit pull the IPAddress/Location and compare against the user's normal interactive sign-in geo/ASN in SigninLogs; a broker sign-in from an IP the user never uses interactively is high suspicion. 2) CONTAIN: If unrecognized, revoke the user's refresh tokens (Revoke-MgUserSignInSession), disable/quarantine any device object registered in the same window, and force re-auth. 3) HUNT: Check AuditLogs for a 'Register device'/'Add device' event by the same user (PRT persistence) and OfficeActivity for inbox-rule or SharePoint/OneDrive bulk download from the broker IP.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| where ApplicationId == "29d9ed98-a469-4536-ade2-f981bc1d605e" or AppDisplayName == "Microsoft Authentication Broker"
| where ResourceDisplayName in ("Device Registration Service","Microsoft Graph")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), SignIns=count(), IPs=make_set(IPAddress,10), Countries=make_set(Country,10) by AccountUpn, AppDisplayName, ResourceDisplayName, ClientAppUsed
| order by FirstSeen desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == 0
| where AppId == "29d9ed98-a469-4536-ade2-f981bc1d605e" or AppDisplayName == "Microsoft Authentication Broker"
| where ResourceDisplayName in ("Device Registration Service","Microsoft Graph")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), SignIns=count(), IPs=make_set(IPAddress,10), Locations=make_set(Location,10) by UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName, ResourceDisplayName, ClientAppUsed
| order by FirstSeen desc

ARToken post-token abuse: inbox rules & SharePoint exfil from device-code sign-in IP AIActions on Objectives Medium
Ties a Microsoft Authentication Broker device-code sign-in to subsequent mailbox rule creation or bulk SharePoint/OneDrive downloads from the SAME source IP — the BEC-automation and SharePoint-exfiltration features Cisco Talos documents in the ARToken EvilTokens panel. Scoping to the broker sign-in IP separates attacker token use from the legitimate user's activity. Rationale: Anchors OfficeActivity/CloudAppEvents inbox-rule and SharePoint/OneDrive download operations to the same source IP that performed the Microsoft Authentication Broker device-code sign-in — matching ARToken's advertised BEC automation + SharePoint exfiltration feature set (Talos), and eliminating the legitimate user's own activity from the same account. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/artoken-inside-an-eviltokens-affiliate-panel-targeting-microsoft-365/ • https://blog.knowbe4.com/warning-artoken-phishing-kit-automates-bec-attacksartoken-phishing-kit-automates-bec-attacks • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/artoken-phaas-exposes-eviltokens-microsoft-365-phishing-toolkit/
ATT&CKT1114.003 T1530 T1567.002
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User legitimately working from home/VPN whose interactive and broker sign-ins share the same IP and who creates a genuine rule
  • Bulk OneDrive sync of a large document library on a newly enrolled device
  • Automated backup/eDiscovery tooling authenticating via broker and downloading files
  • Admin-configured transport/inbox rules pushed during onboarding
  • Legitimate SharePoint site migration from the same egress IP
Suppression filter
// Drop matches where the broker IP is also the user's habitual interactive IP (not attacker infra)
// join kind=leftanti against SigninLogs interactive sign-ins (IsInteractive==true) on UserId+ClientIP before alerting
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Review the make_set of inbox rules and downloaded file names; forwarding-to-external or hide-in-RSS rules plus >50 unique files is high confidence. 2) CONTAIN: Revoke tokens/PRTs, delete malicious inbox rules, disable external forwarding, and block the source IP at CA/named-locations; notify the mailbox owner of potential BEC. 3) HUNT: Enumerate all mailboxes/sites touched from the same ClientIP, check for outbound BEC replies in the thread, and correlate with UC1/UC2 hits for the same principal.
let brokerIPs = AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

| where ApplicationId == "29d9ed98-a469-4536-ade2-f981bc1d605e" or AppDisplayName == "Microsoft Authentication Broker"
| summarize by AccountObjectId, IPAddress;
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("New-InboxRule","Set-InboxRule","FileDownloaded","FileSyncDownloadedFull")
| join kind=inner brokerIPs on AccountObjectId, IPAddress
| summarize Ops=count(), Actions=make_set(ActionType,10), Objects=make_set(ObjectName,10), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp) by AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, Application, IPAddress
| order by Ops desc
let brokerIPs = SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == 0
| where AppId == "29d9ed98-a469-4536-ade2-f981bc1d605e" or AppDisplayName == "Microsoft Authentication Broker"
| summarize by UserId=UserPrincipalName, ClientIP=IPAddress;
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Operation in ("New-InboxRule","Set-InboxRule","FileDownloaded","FileSyncDownloadedFull")
| join kind=inner brokerIPs on UserId, ClientIP
| summarize Ops=count(), Operations=make_set(Operation,10), Files=make_set(SourceFileName,20), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by UserId, OfficeWorkload, ClientIP
| order by Ops desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents

Chinese Hacker Commands DeepSeek via Telegram to Launch Autonomous Attacks

The Hacker News
2026-07-31 10 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42 says a Chinese-speaking threat actor used DeepSeek through the open-source Hermes Agent framework to launch attacks autonomously. After an initial Telegram instruction, the agent found internet-facing systems and selected public exploits. The researchers recovered no further operator input in the session. The operator, tracked through the aliases knaithe and KnYuan,

Hermes/DeepSeek autonomous AI agent artifact: python3 -m http.server 8888 from /home/worker AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the opsec-failure artifact that exposed this campaign: the Hermes Agent (DeepSeek-driven, 'Yolo' unattended mode) launched a Python stdlib file server on port 8888 out of /home/worker, exposing exploit scripts, API keys and session logs. This surfaces the same autonomous-agent tooling running on your own Linux fleet or on a compromised host being used as a staging box. Rationale: Uses the exact opsec artifact Unit 42 named — 'Hermes Agent exposed the operation by starting python3 -m http.server 8888 from /home/worker'. The http.server module + fixed port 8888 combination is the high-fidelity anchor; the /home/worker CWD / 'worker' account is projected as an enrichment flag. Cross-checked Unit 42 and BleepingComputer. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/autonomous-ai-cyber-attack-campaign/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hacker-uses-deepseek-ai-to-autonomously-attack-vulnerable-servers/
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1071.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Data scientist / developer running 'python -m http.server 8888' to quickly share files on a lab host
  • CI runner or container serving build artifacts over the stdlib http server on 8888
  • Internal documentation preview served with http.server on the conventional 8888 port
  • Ad-hoc troubleshooting of a Jupyter-adjacent workflow where 8888 is the habitual port
Suppression filter
| where not (AccountName in~ ("jenkins","gitlab-runner","builder") and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("bash","sh") and ProcessCommandLine has "/build/")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree and shell history around the http.server PID — confirm the CWD and enumerate sibling processes (exploit scripts, curl/wget to FOFA/GitHub, other python agents). Check whether the parent is an interactive shell (benign dev) vs an unattended agent/cron. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the listener, and rotate any API keys/tokens present under the serving directory (Hermes exposed model API keys). 3) Hunt: on the same host look for outbound to FOFA/GitHub raw-content, downloaded public exploit files, and marimo/n8n/langflow scanning cmdlines; sweep the fleet for other :8888 http.server listeners.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("python","python3")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "http.server" and ProcessCommandLine has "8888"
| extend HermesHomeDir = (ProcessCommandLine has "/home/worker" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "/home/worker" or AccountName =~ "worker")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, HermesHomeDir
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("python","python3")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "http.server" and TargetProcessCommandLine has "8888"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcess = ActingProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Marimo CVE-2026-39987 pre-auth RCE: marimo notebook process spawning a shell AIExploitation High
Hunts successful exploitation of the Marimo unauthenticated /terminal/ws WebSocket flaw, where an attacker obtains a root PTY shell. Detection fires when the marimo notebook server process spawns an interactive shell or recon/download binary — the direct post-RCE landing that the agent used to run commands on 11 Marimo instances. Rationale: Corroborated via GitHub advisory GHSA-2679-6mx9-h9xc / Resecurity: the /terminal/ws endpoint skips validate_auth() and hands back a root PTY, so a marimo (python) parent spawning sh/bash/curl is the unambiguous RCE landing. Parent keyed on 'marimo' in cmdline/path; alternative web-log angle is a WebSocket upgrade to /terminal/ws. Datadog left empty — auditd parent-process correlation isn't expressible with the documented Datadog linux.auditd fields. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2679-6mx9-h9xc • https://www.resecurity.com/blog/article/marimo-pre-auth-rce-via-unauthenticated-websocket-terminal-cve-2026-39987 • https://thehackernews.com/2026/04/marimo-rce-flaw-cve-2026-39987.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate notebook code cells that shell out (subprocess/os.system) to run tooling as part of a data pipeline
  • Marimo admin running a terminal deliberately for maintenance
  • Container entrypoint scripts where marimo is the PID 1 wrapper spawning shell helpers on startup
  • CI job that launches marimo and immediately shells to install dependencies
Suppression filter
| where not (ChildProcess in~ ("python","python3") and ChildCmd has "pip install")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the child shell's command line and downstream activity (whoami/id showing root, curl/wget of second-stage payloads). Correlate with a web request to /terminal/ws around the same timestamp and check the source IP against the >460-target scanning infrastructure. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the marimo process and shell, and confirm Marimo is upgraded to >=0.23.0 (fixed build). 3) Hunt: pull all commands run via the PTY, look for persistence (cron, systemd, SSH keys), and sweep for other internet-exposed marimo/notebook interfaces still on vulnerable versions.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "marimo" or InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "marimo" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "marimo"
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","curl","wget","id","whoami","python","python3")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ChildProcess = FileName, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "marimo" or ActingProcessName =~ "marimo"
| where TargetProcessName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","curl","wget","id","whoami","python","python3")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcess = ActingProcessName, ParentCmd = ActingProcessCommandLine, ChildProcess = TargetProcessName, ChildCmd = TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

NetScaler CVE-2026-3055 SAML IdP memory overread: high-volume /saml/login scraping AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts exploitation of the Citrix NetScaler SAML IdP memory-overread flaw used to exfiltrate data from three organizations. A single source repeatedly hits the SAML IdP /saml/login endpoint to leak leftover request memory (session tokens/data) — abnormal versus real users who authenticate once. Applies to customer-managed NetScaler ADC/Gateway configured as a SAML IdP. Rationale: Anchored on the corroborated exploitation primitive: Horizon3/watchTowr/Fortinet confirm CVE-2026-3055 is triggered by repeated requests to the SAML IdP '/saml/login' endpoint (NSC_TASS) to over-read appliance memory, and the article ties this to data exfil from three orgs. A single source hammering /saml/login 100+ times per 10m is the differentiator from legitimate single-shot SAML logins. Defender/Falcon/Datadog left empty — NetScaler appliance web telemetry lands in Sentinel CEF and web-proxy datamodels, not endpoint EDR; Sigma skipped because this is a volumetric/threshold detection. Cross-checked against: • https://horizon3.ai/attack-research/vulnerabilities/cve-2026-3055/ • https://watchtowr.com/resources/rapid-reaction-to-cve-2026-3055/ • https://threat-modeling.com/citrix-netscaler-saml-idp-cve-2026-3055/
ATT&CKT1190 T1552.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A busy legitimate SAML IdP fronting many apps where a NAT/egress gateway concentrates hundreds of real logins behind one SourceIP
  • Uptime/synthetic monitoring repeatedly probing the /saml/login health path
  • Load-testing or SSO integration testing hammering the IdP endpoint
  • A misconfigured SP retry loop re-requesting /saml/login
Suppression filter
| where DistinctUA <= 2 and SourceIP !in ("<corporate_nat_egress_ip>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: profile the top SourceIP — is it a corporate NAT egress (many real users) or a single external/hosting-provider IP with one user-agent and no successful auth follow-through? Inspect response sizes/status for the over-read pattern. 2) Contain: block the source at the NetScaler/WAF, and verify the appliance is on the fixed build (14.1-66.59 / 13.1-62.23 or later); if unpatched and configured as SAML IdP, treat leaked session material as compromised and rotate. 3) Hunt: correlate the SourceIP against inbound access to Langflow/n8n/marimo scanning, and review authenticated sessions from tokens that may have been leaked from appliance memory.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DeviceVendor has "Citrix" or DeviceProduct has_any ("NetScaler","ADC")
| where RequestURL has "/saml/login"
| summarize Requests = count(), DistinctUA = dcount(RequestClientApplication), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), SampleURLs = make_set(RequestURL, 5) by SourceIP, DestinationHostName, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where Requests > 100    // 100+ /saml/login hits from one source in 10m = memory scraping, not a real login
| order by Requests desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`

     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",

| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
