Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")

Network Anomaly Detection in KATA

Securelist (Kaspersky)
2026-07-31 6 use cases 4 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

An analysis of how Network Anomaly Detection (NAD) rules work within Kaspersky Anti Targeted Attack, using Kerberoasting and DNS tunneling attacks as examples.

ATT&CKT1021.001 T1190 T1558 T1558.003
Domainstestinglab.ru crust.testinglab.ru
Click any ATT&CK pill below to open it on the Matrix
Phase 1
Reconnaissance
Detected

Detected

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] DNS tunneling: host issuing many long unique subdomain queries under one parent domain · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains · DNS tunneling / TXT-heavy domain queries
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Kerberoasting: single account/host requesting TGS tickets for many unique non-system SPNs
Kerberoasting: single account/host requesting TGS tickets for many unique non-system SPNs AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the exact anomaly the KATA NAD 'Signs of a Kerberoasting attack' rule targets: one client account (cname) from one source IP receiving successful Kerberos TGS responses for N or more distinct service (non-machine) SPNs inside a short window. System/computer-account SPNs are excluded because they carry uncrackable auto-generated passwords, mirroring the article's excl logic. Fan-out volume, not encryption type, is the signal. Rationale: Anchors on the article's exact NAD logic — KRB_TGS_REP fan-out (dcount of non-'$' ServiceName per requesting cname/source IP) with system SPNs excluded and a count_spns threshold, rather than RC4 signature. MITRE DET0157 independently describes the same 'one account, many distinct SPNs, short window' pattern. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/detectionstrategies/DET0157/ • https://securelist.com/tr/network-anomaly-detection-in-kata/120892/
ATT&CKT1558.003
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Vulnerability scanners (Tenable/Qualys/BloodHound collectors) enumerating SPNs across the domain
  • SCCM/MECM or monitoring service accounts that legitimately touch many services at startup
  • A privileged admin workstation opening many Kerberos-authenticated apps (SQL, CIFS, HTTP) in a burst after logon
  • Backup/inventory tooling that iterates service accounts
  • Login storms after a DC reboot causing batched ticket requests
Suppression filter
| where TargetUserName !in~ ("svc-scanner","svc-bloodhound","svc-sccm") and IpAddress !in ("10.0.0.0/8-scanner-subnet")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pivot on TargetUserName + IpAddress; resolve the source host and confirm whether the account/host normally requests these SPNs. Check if requests came from a workstation vs a server and whether the targeted accounts are high-value (SQL/admin service accounts). 2) Contain: if unsanctioned, disable/force-reset the requesting account and any targeted service-account passwords (assume offline crack in progress), and isolate the source host. 3) Hunt: search for the same source IP performing LDAP SPN enumeration prior to the burst, subsequent logons using the targeted service accounts, and Rubeus/Impacket GetUserSPNs command-line artifacts on the source host.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where EventID == 4769
| where Status == "0x0"                       // successful TGS-REP only (article: KRB_TGS_REP)
| where ServiceName !endswith "$"             // exclude machine/computer-account SPNs (auto-generated strong passwords)
| where ServiceName !in~ ("krbtgt")
| where TargetUserName !endswith "$" and TargetUserName !in~ ("","-")
| summarize UniqueSPNs = dcount(ServiceName), TargetedSPNs = make_set(ServiceName, 25), TGSRequests = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
    by TargetUserName, IpAddress, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where UniqueSPNs >= 10           // count_spns threshold: single account pulling >=10 distinct service SPNs in 10m
| order by UniqueSPNs desc
source:windows.security @EventID:4769 -@TargetUserName:*$
ENDPOINT
`wineventlog_security` EventCode=4769 Service_Name!="*$" Service_Name!="krbtgt" Account_Name!="*$" Failure_Code="0x0"
| eval win=bin(_time, span=10m)
| stats dc(Service_Name) AS unique_spns values(Service_Name) AS targeted_spns count AS tgs_requests min(_time) AS firstTime max(_time) AS lastTime by Account_Name, Client_Address, win
| where unique_spns >= 10
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - unique_spns
DNS tunneling: host issuing many long unique subdomain queries under one parent domain AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the KATA 'Data tunneling in DNS traffic' anomaly: a single host emitting a high volume of unique, abnormally long subdomain labels under one parent zone (encoded data smuggled in the QNAME). Behaviour-based — thresholds on unique-subdomain count and label length rather than a static domain IOC — so it catches the article's example (e.g. crust.testinglab.ru-style beacons) and unknown tunnels alike. Rationale: Anchors on the article's KATA rule shape — per-source high volume of unique subdomains under a single parent zone, with long QNAMEs carrying encoded data — instead of the disposable lab IOC (testinglab.ru / crust.testinglab.ru is a Kaspersky test zone, not shipped as an IOC). MITRE DET0400 corroborates the long-label (>30 char) + abnormal query-volume-to-single-domain signals; thresholds set at 40-char avg / 50 unique labels. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/detectionstrategies/DET0400/ • https://securelist.com/tr/network-anomaly-detection-in-kata/120892/
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1048.003
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • CDN / anti-bot providers (Akamai, Cloudflare, CDN edge tokens) that embed long hashed labels in FQDNs
  • Antivirus/EDR cloud-reputation lookups that hash file/URL data into subdomains (e.g. McAfee, Sophos, Trend)
  • Telemetry/analytics SDKs beaconing device IDs as subdomain labels
  • Email security gateways doing SPF/DKIM/DMARC and RBL lookups in bulk
  • Legitimate DNS-based licensing or software-update check-ins with encoded tokens
Suppression filter
| where Parent !endswith "akamaiedge.net" and Parent !endswith "cloudflare.com" and Parent !endswith "trafficmanager.net" and Parent !endswith "amazonaws.com"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the parent zone and the initiating process/host; check domain age/registration and whether the zone is a known CDN/security vendor. Inspect sample QNAMEs for base32/base64/hex encoding and consistent length. 2) Contain: if the zone is unrecognised, sinkhole/block it at the resolver and isolate the source host; capture the process making the queries. 3) Hunt: pivot to other hosts querying the same parent zone, correlate to a non-browser/non-system parent process (powershell/rundll32/python) initiating the DNS, and look for matching TXT/NULL/CNAME record types indicative of a tunnel utility (iodine, dnscat2).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1h)
| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| extend Labels = split(RemoteUrl, ".")
| where array_length(Labels) >= 3
| extend Parent = strcat(tostring(Labels[array_length(Labels)-2]), ".", tostring(Labels[array_length(Labels)-1]))
| where Parent !endswith "in-addr.arpa"
| summarize UniqueFqdns = dcount(RemoteUrl), AvgLen = avg(strlen(RemoteUrl)), MaxLen = max(strlen(RemoteUrl)), Conns = count(), Sample = make_set(RemoteUrl, 10)
    by DeviceName, Parent, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where UniqueFqdns >= 50 and AvgLen >= 40    // 50 distinct long labels under one zone in 10m = tunneling shape
| order by UniqueFqdns desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where isnotempty(Name)
| where Name !endswith ".in-addr.arpa" and Name !endswith ".arpa"
| extend Labels = split(Name, ".")
| where array_length(Labels) >= 3
| extend Parent = strcat(tostring(Labels[array_length(Labels)-2]), ".", tostring(Labels[array_length(Labels)-1]))
| extend TopLabelLen = strlen(tostring(Labels[0]))
| summarize UniqueSubdomains = dcount(Name), QueryCount = count(), AvgLen = avg(strlen(Name)), MaxTopLabel = max(TopLabelLen), Sample = make_set(Name, 10)
    by ClientIP, Parent, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where UniqueSubdomains >= 50 and AvgLen >= 40   // MITRE DET0400: many long unique labels to one zone
| order by UniqueSubdomains desc
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/.{40,}/
| regex("(?<parent>[a-z0-9-]+\.[a-z]+)$", field=DomainName)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, parent], function=[count(field=DomainName, distinct=true, as=unique_long_subdomains), count(as=total_queries)])
| unique_long_subdomains >= 50
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count AS query_count, dc(DNS.query) AS unique_subdomains, values(DNS.query) AS sample_queries FROM datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS WHERE nodename=DNS DNS.message_type="QUERY" BY DNS.src, DNS.query, _time span=10m
| eval parent=replace(DNS.query, "^.*?\.([^.]+\.[^.]+)$", "\1"), qlen=len(DNS.query)
| stats sum(query_count) AS total_queries, dc(DNS.query) AS unique_subdomains, avg(qlen) AS avg_len, max(qlen) AS max_len, values(sample_queries) AS sample_queries BY DNS.src, parent
| where unique_subdomains >= 50 AND avg_len >= 40
| sort - unique_subdomains
| tstats summariesonly=false count AS query_count, dc(DNS.query) AS unique_subdomains, values(DNS.query) AS sample_queries FROM datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS WHERE nodename=DNS DNS.message_type="QUERY" BY DNS.src, DNS.query, _time span=10m
| eval parent=replace(DNS.query, "^.*?\.([^.]+\.[^.]+)$", "\1"), qlen=len(DNS.query)
| stats sum(query_count) AS total_queries, dc(DNS.query) AS unique_subdomains, avg(qlen) AS avg_len, max(qlen) AS max_len, values(sample_queries) AS sample_queries BY DNS.src, parent
| where unique_subdomains >= 50 AND avg_len >= 40
| sort - unique_subdomains
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

XCSSET v40 CDP hijack: Google Chrome launched with remote-debugging-port AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the XCSSET v40 Chrome-hijacking module activating the Chrome DevTools Protocol by relaunching the legitimate Google Chrome binary with --remote-debugging-port (and, post-Chrome-136, a non-default --user-data-dir) so the dropped chrome_remote binary can attach to the browser engine. Article-specific because it targets the exact CDP-enablement command line the wrapper uses on the real Chrome binary, not headless automation. Rationale: Uses the article's exact CDP-enablement behaviour (legitimate 'Google Chrome' binary + --remote-debugging-port, with --user-data-dir surfaced because Chrome 136+ ignores the switch on the default profile). Cross-checked against MITRE S0658 and vendor write-ups confirming the CDP module. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0658/ • https://www.securityweek.com/new-xcsset-macos-malware-variant-hijacks-cryptocurrency-transactions/ • https://thehackernews.com/2025/09/new-macos-xcsset-variant-targets.html
ATT&CKT1185 T1539 T1554
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers running Selenium/Puppeteer/Playwright test suites that launch Chrome with a debugging port
  • chromedriver-driven CI/automation on developer laptops
  • Manual QA using `--remote-debugging-port` for front-end debugging
  • VS Code / JS debugger 'attach to Chrome' launch configs
  • Lighthouse / performance-profiling tooling launching Chrome with CDP
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chromedriver","node","python","python3","Code Helper") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "puppeteer" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "selenium"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the launching parent — automation binaries (chromedriver/node/python) are benign; a shell, osascript, or unknown wrapper parenting real 'Google Chrome' with a debugging port is suspicious. Check for a chrome_remote binary or a 'boot' process on the same host in the same window. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the Chrome + chrome_remote processes, and force-revoke/rotate browser session cookies and any SSO tokens (CDP theft is invisible to the user). 3) Hunt: pivot to all Xcode projects on the host for injected loader scripts, look for the C2 URI paths (/s/, /d/, /l, /u) in proxy logs, and check other developer endpoints that cloned the same repo.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName =~ "Google Chrome"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--remote-debugging-port"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chromedriver","node","python","python3")
| extend UsesCustomProfile = iff(ProcessCommandLine has "--user-data-dir", "yes", "no")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, ParentProcess=InitiatingProcessFileName, ParentCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, UsesCustomProfile, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where TargetProcessName has "Google Chrome"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "--remote-debugging-port"
| where ActingProcessName !has "chromedriver" and ActingProcessName !has "node" and ActingProcessName !has "python"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

XCSSET v40 chrome_remote backdoor execution and C2 WebSocket egress AICommand & Control High
Hunts the dropped chrome_remote Mach-O binary that XCSSET v40 uses to attach to the opened CDP port and open a persistent WebSocket to the rotating C2 for real-time JavaScript injection and cookie exfiltration. High fidelity because chrome_remote is a unique, article-named binary that should never exist on a clean macOS host. Rationale: Pivots on the article's uniquely named chrome_remote binary (the CDP-attach/WebSocket-C2 component) — a name absent from any legitimate macOS install, giving a low-FP, high-confidence signal. Corroborated by MITRE S0658 and vendor reporting describing the CDP cookie-theft backdoor. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0658/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/ • https://www.securityweek.com/new-xcsset-macos-malware-variant-hijacks-cryptocurrency-transactions/
ATT&CKT1185 T1071.001 T1539 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Extremely rare — no legitimate macOS software ships a binary named chrome_remote
  • A developer's own project artifact coincidentally named chrome_remote (check code-signing/notarization and path)
  • Security researcher detonating XCSSET samples in a lab
  • An unrelated 'Chrome Remote Desktop' component (verify full path/signature — the real one is 'chrome-remote-desktop', not 'chrome_remote')
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the chrome_remote path and SHA256, verify it is unsigned/un-notarized and dropped outside a normal app bundle; confirm whether it made outbound connections and to which host. 2) Contain: isolate the endpoint, terminate chrome_remote and its parent Chrome, block the resolved C2 IP/domain at the proxy, and invalidate all browser sessions and OAuth tokens for the user. 3) Hunt: search the fleet for the same SHA256, for Chrome launched with --remote-debugging-port (UC1), and for infected Xcode projects/loader scripts that would re-drop the binary on the next build.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName =~ "chrome_remote" or FolderPath endswith "/chrome_remote"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, ParentProcess=InitiatingProcessFileName, ParentCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where TargetProcessName has "chrome_remote"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

XCSSET v40 build-triggered loader: Xcode build spawning osascript/curl AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the XCSSET v40 initial infection that fires only when a developer builds an infected Xcode project locally — the injected loader runs from an Xcode Run-Script build phase and spawns osascript or curl to reach the C2 and stage further modules. Article-specific because it targets the Xcode/xcodebuild build-tree ancestry that is XCSSET's signature delivery vector. Rationale: Grounded in the article's core delivery mechanic — infection triggers when the developer builds the infected Xcode project, with an AppleScript/curl loader establishing C2. Ancestry on xcodebuild/Xcode + osascript/curl is XCSSET-specific and distinct from generic script execution. Cross-checked against MITRE S0658. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0658/ • https://thehackernews.com/2025/09/new-macos-xcsset-variant-targets.html
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1059.002 T1071.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • CocoaPods / Swift Package Manager or fastlane Run-Script phases that curl dependencies during a build
  • SwiftLint / build scripts using osascript to post notifications or display dialogs
  • In-house build automation that pings a webhook via curl on build completion
  • Crashlytics/Sentry dSYM upload scripts invoking curl from a build phase
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("cocoapods","github.com","swiftpm","fastlane","crashlytics","sentry-cli"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the ProcessCommandLine of the osascript/curl child — benign build tooling references known package hosts (cocoapods.org, github.com dependency URLs); XCSSET reaches short single-letter C2 paths (/a, /s/, /d/) and base64 payloads. Inspect the offending Xcode project's build phases for an injected script. 2) Contain: quarantine the project/repo, isolate the endpoint if C2 contact is confirmed, and block the destination host. 3) Hunt: check whether Chrome was subsequently launched with --remote-debugging-port (UC1) or chrome_remote executed (UC2), and identify every other developer who cloned/built the same repo to scope worming across projects.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName in~ ("osascript","curl")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("xcodebuild","Xcode")
    or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("xcodebuild","Xcode")
    or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any (".xcodeproj",".xcworkspace","DerivedData","Build/Intermediates.noindex")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, Parent=InitiatingProcessFileName, ParentCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, GrandParent=InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("osascript","curl")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("xcodebuild","Xcode") or ParentProcessName has_any ("xcodebuild","Xcode") or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (".xcodeproj",".xcworkspace","DerivedData")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",

                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")

AWS Amplify UI Builder CreateComponent/UpdateComponent — CVE-2025-4318 malicious schema injection AIInstallation Medium
Hunts AmplifyUIBuilder CreateComponent/UpdateComponent/ExportComponent CloudTrail events, the exact API path an authenticated principal uses to import a component schema whose property bindings carry arbitrary JavaScript (CVE-2025-4318). The injected expression re-executes during every codegen/render/build, so the create/update call is the persistence-planting event to surface and attribute to a principal + source IP. Rationale: Uses the concrete eventSource amplifyuibuilder.amazonaws.com and the CreateComponent/UpdateComponent/ExportComponent API names named in the advisory (and confirmed in the AmplifyUIBuilder API reference) — the exact and only path a malicious component schema is imported through. Cross-checked against: • https://aws.amazon.com/security/security-bulletins/AWS-2025-010/ • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amplifyuibuilder/latest/APIReference/API_CreateComponent.html • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/@aws-amplify/codegen-ui-react/CVE-2025-4318/
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1195.002
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate developers building/editing UI Builder components in Amplify Studio during normal front-end development
  • Amplify Studio auto-generating components from a DataStore/GraphQL schema import
  • CI service role programmatically syncing components as part of an IaC/export workflow
  • QA or design teams iterating on forms/views/themes
  • First-time Amplify Studio onboarding generating starter components in bulk
Suppression filter
| where userIdentity.type != "AssumedRole" or requestParameters.name has_any ("eval","constructor","process","require","${")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the userIdentity.arn, sourceIPAddress and componentName; confirm the principal is an expected Amplify developer and the IP/geo matches normal dev activity. Retrieve the component schema (GetComponent) and inspect bindingProperties/collectionProperties for expression-like or JS payloads (e.g. constructor, process, require, backtick/${} expressions). 2) Contain: if the schema contains code, delete/roll back the component, rotate the principal's credentials, and freeze codegen builds that pull it (amplify pull / ampx) until packages are on @aws-amplify/codegen-ui(-react) >= 2.20.4. 3) Hunt: enumerate all CreateComponent/UpdateComponent by that principal, check build-host/CI process telemetry for anomalous node child processes at codegen time, and inventory repos for vulnerable codegen-ui versions <=2.20.2.

AWS Amplify UI Builder create-component CLI invocation on endpoint/CI host (CVE-2025-4318) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts process executions of the AWS CLI 'amplifyuibuilder create-component/update-component/export-component' commands on developer workstations and CI/build runners — the client-side action that imports a component schema and (for vulnerable <=2.20.2 codegen-ui) triggers arbitrary JavaScript during local codegen/build. Complements the CloudTrail UC by catching the on-host command line and its parent process. Rationale: Anchors on the exact 'create-component' command named in the advisory (plus the update/export variants that share the vulnerable binding path) scoped by the 'amplifyuibuilder' service token, so it fires only on Amplify UI Builder schema imports rather than generic AWS CLI usage. Cross-checked against: • https://aws.amazon.com/security/security-bulletins/AWS-2025-010/ • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amplifyuibuilder/latest/APIReference/API_CreateComponent.html
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Front-end developers legitimately importing/exporting components via aws amplifyuibuilder in local dev
  • CI/CD pipeline steps that scriptaws amplifyuibuilder export-component for codegen
  • Infrastructure-as-code sync jobs recreating components from JSON definitions
  • Amplify migration/backup scripts bulk-exporting components
  • Automated tests that provision throwaway components
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("jenkins-agent.exe","runner.worker.exe","buildkitd.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full ProcessCommandLine and any --cli-input-json / --component-to-create payload path; open the referenced schema and inspect property bindings for JS (eval, constructor, require, ${}, backticks). Confirm whether the host's node_modules ships @aws-amplify/codegen-ui(-react) <=2.20.2. 2) Contain: on a confirmed malicious schema, isolate the build host/CI runner, kill child node/codegen processes, and block the build from publishing artifacts; upgrade codegen-ui to >=2.20.4 before re-running. 3) Hunt: correlate to the CloudTrail CreateComponent/UpdateComponent event by the same identity/time, review that principal's other Amplify actions, and sweep all build hosts for the vulnerable package version.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "amplifyuibuilder"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("create-component","update-component","export-component")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "amplifyuibuilder"
| where CommandLine has_any ("create-component","update-component","export-component")
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Install of compromised @joyfill/components or @joyfill/layouts 2773 beta versions AIDelivery High
Hunts npm/yarn/pnpm install or lockfile writes pulling @joyfill/components or @joyfill/layouts prerelease versions carrying the '2773' campaign marker. These specific beta tarballs ship an obfuscated RAT that runs on import, so any presence on a developer machine or CI runner is a compromise. Rationale: Anchors on the article's exact package names (@joyfill/components, @joyfill/layouts) plus the shared '2773' beta campaign marker that appears in every compromised version string (4.0.0-rc24-2773-beta.x, 0.1.2-2773.beta.x), making it near-zero-FP.

  • Automated IOC-scanning tooling that echoes the package string in its own command line

| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "sandbox" and DeviceName !startswith "MALWARE-LAB"

node.exe spawns detached 'node -e' second-stage loader (joyfill RAT) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts a node.exe process spawning a child node.exe with an inline -e/--eval payload, matching the joyfill implant's detached second-stage that requests /$/boot from a second host and XOR-decrypts the response. node spawning node -e is rare in normal application runtime. Rationale: The article states the implant 'spawns a detached node -e child that requests /$/boot from a second host', so node->node -e is the concrete process-tree signature of the obfuscated second stage rather than a generic eval template.
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Build tooling (webpack/vite plugins, node scripts) legitimately using node -e for one-liners
  • Test harnesses spawning node -e to evaluate assertions
  • CI pipeline steps that invoke node --eval for version/env checks
  • Monorepo task runners shelling out to node -e
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "\\node_modules\\.bin\\" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "webpack"
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full child command line and any URL/IP it references; correlate the parent node.exe working directory against node_modules/@joyfill. 2) Contain: kill the detached node process, isolate host, block the second-stage host at egress. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host for outbound connections to the joyfill C2 IPs and /$/boot path, and for the persistence file writes into developer-tool modules.

Joyfill RAT C2 callout to hardcoded IPs and /$/boot request paths AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on outbound connections to the joyfill implant's four hardcoded C2 IPs, or HTTP requests to its distinctive Socket.IO/boot paths (/$/boot, /u/e, /u/f, /0x/js, /verify-human/, /snv). These are the RAT's phone-home and second-stage retrieval channels. Rationale: Uses the four exact C2 IPs (166.88.134.62, 23.27.13.43, 198.105.127.210, 23.27.202.27) and the six documented request paths (/$/boot etc.) directly from the article's IOC section — dedicated infrastructure with negligible legitimate use.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1095
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A threat-intel/IOC validation scan reaching the C2 IPs from a sanctioned scanner host
  • IP reassignment after takedown to a benign hosting tenant (stale IOC)
  • A generic /snv or /u/e path collision on an unrelated internal web app (path clause only, not the IP clause)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("nessus.exe","tenable.exe") and DeviceName !startswith "SCANNER-"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process — node.exe or an injected developer tool (Discord/VS Code/GitHub Desktop) indicates active RAT; confirm which IP/path fired. 2) Contain: block all four IPs at the perimeter, isolate the host, kill the node/injected process. 3) Hunt: rotate credentials on the workstation, search for the staged Python infostealer and encrypted archive exfil, and check other hosts that imported @joyfill for the same beacons.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("166.88.134.62","23.27.13.43","198.105.127.210","23.27.202.27")
   or RemoteUrl has_any ("/$/boot","/u/e","/u/f","/0x/js","/verify-human/","/snv")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr in ("166.88.134.62","23.27.13.43","198.105.127.210","23.27.202.27")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, Url
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Joyfill RAT persistence: node.exe rewrites @vscode/deviceid, Discord core, GitHub Desktop main.js, npm CLI AIInstallation High
Detects node.exe modifying developer-tool modules the joyfill implant injects a self-reloading block into: @vscode/deviceid (VS Code/Cursor/Antigravity), Discord desktop core, GitHub Desktop main.js, and the global npm CLI. Legitimate updates to these files come from installers/Update.exe, not node.exe. Rationale: Maps exactly to the article's named persistence targets (@vscode/deviceid, Discord desktop core module, GitHub Desktop main.js, global npm CLI) and constrains the writer to node.exe, which does not legitimately patch these installed application files.
ATT&CKT1546 T1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer running a legitimate node-based patch/postinstall script that rewrites npm-cli.js during an npm self-update
  • Electron app dev builds regenerating main.js in a local GitHubDesktop clone
  • A monorepo tool touching @vscode/deviceid during VS Code extension development
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "npm-lifecycle" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "electron-rebuild"
Response runbook
1) Triage: diff the modified module against a clean copy to confirm the injected self-reloading block / '9-0135-3' marker; identify the parent node process and its package context. 2) Contain: isolate the host, restore the affected developer-tool files from known-good installs, remove @joyfill packages. 3) Hunt: because persistence survives package removal, sweep all developer machines for the same modified files and for RAT C2 beacons; rotate developer credentials.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileModified","FileCreated")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe"
| where FolderPath has @"\@vscode\deviceid"
   or FolderPath has "discord_desktop_core"
   or (FileName =~ "main.js" and FolderPath has "GitHubDesktop")
   or FileName =~ "npm-cli.js"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName endswith "node.exe"
| where TargetFilePath has @"\@vscode\deviceid"
   or TargetFilePath has "discord_desktop_core"
   or (TargetFileName =~ "main.js" and TargetFilePath has "GitHubDesktop")
   or TargetFileName =~ "npm-cli.js"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Joyfill Python credential stealer spawned by node.exe AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts node.exe spawning a Python interpreter that reaches into browser data, extension wallets/password managers, and OS keychains — the joyfill implant's staged infostealer. A JS runtime launching Python that touches credential stores is highly abnormal for legitimate node apps. Rationale: The article states the implant 'stages a Python infostealer that collects browser data, extension wallets and password managers, Git/GitHub CLI credentials, and OS keychains' — node.exe as parent of a Python interpreter is the article-specific process lineage for that stage.
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A node-based dev tool invoking a Python helper script (e.g. node-gyp calling python for native module builds)
  • ML/data tooling where a Node front-end shells out to Python
  • node-based test runners orchestrating Python integration tests
  • Editor extensions bundling a Python language server launched via node
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "node-gyp" and ProcessCommandLine !has_any ("gyp","build","language-server")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the Python command line and any files it opened (browser Login Data, wallet extension dirs, keychains); confirm the node parent's package context. 2) Contain: kill the Python process, isolate the host, block C2 egress to prevent archive upload. 3) Hunt: treat all credentials on the machine as stolen and rotate (browser, Git/GitHub CLI, wallets, keychains); search for the encrypted archive creation and outbound POST to the joyfill C2.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("python.exe","python3.exe","pythonw.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "node.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("python.exe","python3.exe","pythonw.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: node.exe spawns Python interpreter (joyfill infostealer stage)

Node.js resolving C2 via public blockchain RPC endpoints (Tron/BSC/Aptos) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunting query for a node.exe process contacting public blockchain RPC endpoints (api.trongrid.io, bsc-dataseed.binance.org, bsc-rpc.publicnode.com, fullnode.mainnet.aptoslabs.com) — the joyfill implant's on-chain C2 resolution that reads a Tron transaction, follows it to a BSC transaction, and evaluates the decrypted input as JavaScript. Rationale: The article describes C2 resolution 'through a public blockchain transaction' reading a Tron address then a BSC transaction via eth_getTransactionByHash; the IOC block lists api.trongrid.io, bsc-dataseed.binance.org, bsc-rpc.publicnode.com and fullnode.mainnet.aptoslabs.com — scoping to node.exe cuts the legitimate crypto-app noise.
ATT&CKT1102.001 T1568
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate Node.js blockchain/web3 application (dApp backend, wallet service, indexer) querying these public RPCs
  • A developer testing a Tron/BSC integration locally with node
  • CI jobs for a crypto project that ping RPC seeds for health checks
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "\\node_modules\\@joyfill\\" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("@joyfill","2773")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the host runs any legitimate web3/blockchain workload; check the node process's package directory for @joyfill and the '9-0135-3' marker. 2) Contain: if no crypto workload is expected, isolate the host and block the RPC endpoints for that process. 3) Hunt: correlate with the /$/boot second-stage retrieval and the hardcoded C2 IPs; rotate credentials and check peers that imported @joyfill.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe"
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("api.trongrid.io","bsc-dataseed.binance.org","bsc-rpc.publicnode.com","fullnode.mainnet.aptoslabs.com")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), Endpoints=make_set(RemoteUrl), Conns=count() by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has_any ("api.trongrid.io","bsc-dataseed.binance.org","bsc-rpc.publicnode.com","fullnode.mainnet.aptoslabs.com")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), Queries=make_set(DnsQuery), Count=count() by SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr
| order by FirstSeen desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`

| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest

DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"

| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)

                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High
Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"

SecurityEvent

status: experimental

    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18", "36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c", "cb46f12d70824ea24ed1f8bcf45bf3f86680e02a9089aafc03b27f691be57be3") or SHA1 in~ ("26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18", "36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c", "cb46f12d70824ea24ed1f8bcf45bf3f86680e02a9089aafc03b27f691be57be3") or MD5 in~ ("26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18", "36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c", "cb46f12d70824ea24ed1f8bcf45bf3f86680e02a9089aafc03b27f691be57be3")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18", "36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c", "cb46f12d70824ea24ed1f8bcf45bf3f86680e02a9089aafc03b27f691be57be3") or SHA1 in~ ("26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18", "36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c", "cb46f12d70824ea24ed1f8bcf45bf3f86680e02a9089aafc03b27f691be57be3") or MD5 in~ ("26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18", "36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c", "cb46f12d70824ea24ed1f8bcf45bf3f86680e02a9089aafc03b27f691be57be3")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18", "36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c", "cb46f12d70824ea24ed1f8bcf45bf3f86680e02a9089aafc03b27f691be57be3"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Article-specific behavioural hunt — Compromised npm Packages: @joyfill/components and @joyfill/layouts Ship an Obfus Exploitation High
Auto-generated hunt targeting the specific binaries, paths, registry locations and command-line fragments named in this article. Hunting tier — needs analyst review and environment tuning before promotion to alerting.
ATT&CKT1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Registry
// Article-specific bespoke detection — Compromised npm Packages: @joyfill/components and @joyfill/layouts Ship an Obfus
// Hunts the actual binaries / paths / commandline fragments named
// in the article instead of a generic technique-class template.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName in~ ("node.js", "esm.js", "min.js", "cjs.js", "main.js"))

Rails web process reads /proc/self/environ or app secrets (Active Storage libvips file-read) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the core arbitrary-file-read primitive of CVE-2026-66066: a crafted upload drives an unfuzzed libvips loader inside the Ruby/Puma process to read the process environment and Rails secrets (secret_key_base, master.key, credentials.yml.enc). Because libvips is linked into the app process, the read shows up as the web-app binary opening files it never touches at runtime. Rationale: Anchored on the exact read targets the GHSA names as the payoff (secret_key_base in the process environment, master.key, credentials.yml.enc) and scoped to the Ruby web-app process as the actor — that pairing is the file-read primitive itself, not a generic file-access rule. Confirmed via the advisory plus Ethiack and Flatt write-ups that the impact is disclosure of the process environment. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xr9x-r78c-5hrm • https://ethiack.com/info-hub/research/kindarails2shell-rails-rce-cve • https://blog.flatt.tech/entry/kindarails2shell_rails • https://www.libvips.org/2022/05/28/What's-new-in-8.13.html
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Rails app legitimately reading config/master.key and config/credentials.yml.enc at boot (normal startup — not /proc/self/environ)
  • Backup or DLP agents reading /etc/passwd during scheduled scans
  • APM/observability agents (e.g. Datadog, New Relic) reading /proc/<pid>/environ for metadata enrichment
  • Config-management runs (Ansible/Chef) reading /etc/passwd or .env files
  • Container init scripts sourcing .env files at container start
Suppression filter
| where not (TargetFilePath has_any ("/config/master.key","/config/credentials.yml.enc") and ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("rails server","puma","bootsnap"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the actor is the web-app process (ruby/puma) and the read occurred mid-request (not at process start) — correlate the read timestamp against Active Storage variant/representation requests in the web/access log. 2) Contain: if /proc/self/environ or /etc/passwd was read by the app process, treat secret_key_base and every env-resident credential as exposed — rotate secret_key_base, master.key, DB creds and S3/GCS/Azure Active Storage keys immediately (invalidates sessions). 3) Hunt: check for follow-on ruby-spawned shells and outbound connections from the host, and search web logs for the uploads that preceded the read (/rails/active_storage/representations/ and /rails/active_storage/direct_uploads).

| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType == "FileAccessed"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("ruby","puma","passenger","rails")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/proc/self/environ","/environ","/etc/passwd","/config/master.key","/config/credentials.yml.enc","/.env")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessId, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ruby/Puma Rails web process spawns a shell (post-file-read RCE via forged secret_key_base cookie) AIExploitation Medium
Detects the RCE stage of CVE-2026-66066: after leaking secret_key_base, the attacker forges a signed/encrypted Rails cookie carrying a deserialization payload, yielding code execution inside the app process. Surfaces the anomalous child — an interactive shell or download tool spawned by the Ruby/Puma web worker. Rationale: The advisory states the file-read escalates to RCE via secrets in the process environment; the observable outcome is the Rails worker (ruby/puma/passenger) spawning a shell or fetch tool — a parent→child pair that is abnormal for a web app running the in-process :vips processor. Parents and children are all concrete binary names, no placeholders. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xr9x-r78c-5hrm • https://blog.flatt.tech/entry/kindarails2shell_rails
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1190 T1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Rails apps that legitimately shell out via system()/backticks (e.g. running git, imagemagick/mini_magick, ffmpeg, or a rake task)
  • Deploy/boot scripts where puma is launched by a shell wrapper and re-execs sh
  • Health-check or cron jobs invoking curl/wget from within the app container
  • Background job workers (Sidekiq/Resque under ruby) shelling out to CLI tools by design
  • Container entrypoints where bundle exec spawns sh for pre-boot hooks
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/dev/tcp","-i ","sh -c","bash -c","-c 'curl","-c \"curl","base64 -d") or ProcessCommandLine !has_any ("git","convert","mogrify","ffmpeg","rake")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect ProcessCommandLine of the child — reverse-shell markers (/dev/tcp, -i, bash -c with piped curl) or interactive shells with no args are high-confidence; benign shell-outs name a specific tool/arg. Correlate against UC1 file-read hits on the same host. 2) Contain: isolate the host/pod, kill the offending Ruby worker, and rotate secret_key_base + all env-resident credentials (the RCE path depends on the leaked signing key). 3) Hunt: pull the preceding web requests to /rails/active_storage/representations/ and /rails/active_storage/direct_uploads, review outbound connections from the host, and check for persistence (cron, authorized_keys, new services).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ruby","ruby3.2","ruby3.3","puma","passenger","bundle","rails")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","nc","ncat","curl","wget","python","python3","perl")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, ProcessId
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("ruby","puma","passenger","bundle","rails")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","/zsh","/nc","/ncat","/curl","/wget","/python","/perl")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Internet-facing hosts running activestorage vulnerable to CVE-2026-66066 AIExploitation High
Exposure hunt for the attack surface: hosts with an activestorage version affected by CVE-2026-66066 (< 7.2.3.2, 8.0.x < 8.0.5.1, 8.1.x < 8.1.3.1), prioritising internet-facing systems and those still on libvips < 8.13 which cannot block unfuzzed loaders. Drives patch/mitigation before the 2026-08-28 full disclosure. Rationale: Uses the exact CVE id and the vendor-published affected-version boundaries from the advisory; joining internet-facing status turns a raw inventory list into a ranked remediation queue for the specific gem in this CVE. No version-string math needed — the TVM CveId already encodes the affected ranges. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xr9x-r78c-5hrm
ATT&CKT1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Hosts already patched to 7.2.3.2 / 8.0.5.1 / 8.1.3.1 but TVM inventory not yet refreshed (stale)
  • Apps that carry ruby-vips only for image analysis and never generate variants (lower real risk despite matching)
  • Hosts where libvips >= 8.13 is present and VIPS_BLOCK_UNTRUSTED / Vips.block_untrusted(true) is already set (mitigated without gem upgrade)
  • Non-production/staging boxes flagged as internet-facing by network heuristics but actually firewalled
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each hit confirm variant_processor is :vips (default since load_defaults 7.0) and whether the app accepts uploads from untrusted users — those two conditions gate real exploitability. 2) Contain: upgrade activestorage to the fixed release and ensure libvips >= 8.13; where an immediate upgrade isn't possible, set VIPS_BLOCK_UNTRUSTED=1 (or Vips.block_untrusted(true)) as an interim block, prioritising internet-facing hosts. 3) Hunt: on any host that was exposed before patching, assume secret exposure — rotate secret_key_base, master.key, DB and Active Storage service credentials, and run UC1/UC2 retrospectively over the exposure window.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where CveId == "CVE-2026-66066"
| join kind=leftouter (DeviceInfo | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, IsInternetFacing, OSPlatform) by DeviceId) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, RecommendedSecurityUpdate, IsInternetFacing, OSPlatform
| order by IsInternetFacing desc, DeviceName asc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId == "CVE-2026-66066"
| join kind=leftouter (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d) | summarize arg_max(TimeGenerated, IsInternetFacing, OSPlatform) by DeviceId) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, RecommendedSecurityUpdate, IsInternetFacing, OSPlatform
| order by IsInternetFacing desc

DPRK-Linked macOS Malvertising Uses Fake Updates to Deliver Crypto-Stealing Malware

The Hacker News
2026-07-30 20 use cases 13 techniques 7 kill-chain phases detected

A lot of security still comes down to trusting the wrong screen. This week, that screen might be a login page, an install guide, a recruiter call, or a familiar service behaving slightly wrong. Behind it: reused credentials, exposed systems, quiet loaders, abused trust, and exploit paths that should have been harder. Some defenses improved. The loose parts still got found first. Anyway,
