ClickFix rundll32 ordinal (#1) execution of non-DLL payload over WebDAV @SSL AIExploitation High
Hunts the CyberProof-tracked ClickFix variant where a pasted Run-dialog command mounts an attacker WebDAV share (\\host@SSL\GUID) and uses rundll32.exe to load a non-DLL file (gc.key, j.pm, goog.ct) by ordinal export #1. Article-specific because it keys on the payload filenames plus the rundll32 ',#1' + '@SSL' WebDAV UNC combination rather than generic rundll32 abuse. Rationale: Keys on the three verbatim payload filenames (gc.key/j.pm/goog.ct) and the rundll32 ',#1' ordinal-load plus '@SSL' WebDAV UNC syntax quoted in the CyberProof write-up — a combination that does not occur in benign rundll32 usage, which always references a real .dll by exported name. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cyberproof.com/blog/clickfix-keeps-evolving-rundll32-ordinal-execution-over-webdav/ • https://gbhackers.com/rundll32-and-webdav/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/new-clickfix-variant-uses-rundll32/
ATT&CKT1218.011 T1204.004 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate software installers that call rundll32 with a real DLL export happen to contain the literal token '#1' in an unrelated argument (rare — no @SSL/payload-name overlap)
  • Internal red-team / purple-team ClickFix simulations reusing the public payload names
  • Security tooling detonating the sample in a sandbox that shares the production Defender workspace
  • A file share genuinely named with '@SSL' in its path (uncommon; WebDAV-over-HTTPS UNC is almost never used interactively)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msiexec.exe","setup.exe") and ProcessCommandLine !has "@SSL" and ProcessCommandLine !has_any ("gc.key","j.pm","goog.ct"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the full ProcessCommandLine and parent chain (explorer.exe->powershell/pcalua/cmd->rundll32). Extract the WebDAV host from the '\\host@SSL' UNC and the payload filename; check DeviceNetworkEvents for the 443/WebDAV connection to that host. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, block the WebDAV domain at proxy/DNS, and kill/quarantine any child processes rundll32 spawned. Reset the user's credentials if hands-on-keyboard follow-on is seen. 3) HUNT: Sweep the org for rundll32 loading any non-.dll file by ordinal '#1', for WebClient service starts, and for the same WebDAV domains across all endpoints; review clipboard/Run-dialog (RunMRU) history on the victim.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "rundll32.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "#1"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("gc.key", "j.pm", "goog.ct") or ProcessCommandLine has "@SSL"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\rundll32.exe"
| where CommandLine has "#1"
| where CommandLine has_any ("gc.key", "j.pm", "goog.ct") or CommandLine has "@SSL"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

MacSync fake-Claude Terminal one-liner: curl piped to zsh via base64 -D AIDelivery High
Hunts the Huntress-documented MacSync initial-access step where a victim pastes a Terminal one-liner (curl -kfsSL $(echo <b64>|base64 -D)|zsh) that resolves to agenticsora[.]com or malwareaudit[.]com /curl/<token> and executes the stage-1 zsh loader. Article-specific because it pins on the exact delivery domains and the base64-decode-then-pipe-to-zsh shape rather than generic curl usage. Rationale: Uses the two verbatim delivery domains (agenticsora[.]com, malwareaudit[.]com) from the Huntress reversing plus the distinctive 'curl ... $(...|base64 -D)|zsh' construction — legitimate macOS install guides fetch signed .dmg/.pkg files, they do not base64-decode a URL and pipe HTTP to the shell. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/macsync-stealer-rat-reverse-engineering • https://cybersecuritynews.com/fake-claude-code-install-guide/ • https://gbhackers.com/fake-claude-code-installer-3/
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.004 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer legitimately using curl|zsh for a trusted install script (e.g. Homebrew, oh-my-zsh) — excluded by the domain/base64-decode anchors
  • Internal macOS provisioning tooling that pipes remote scripts to a shell (should not reference the attacker domains)
  • Security researcher intentionally detonating the MacSync sample
  • CI runners on macOS fetching bootstrap scripts (won't match the specific domains or the base64 -D wrapper)
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("brew.sh", "raw.githubusercontent.com", "install.sh") and ProcessCommandLine !has_any ("agenticsora.com","malwareaudit.com"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Capture the full ProcessCommandLine and decode the base64 blob to confirm the /curl/<token> endpoint; check for the follow-on zsh loader and a persistence line appended to ~/.zshrc. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the Mac, block agenticsora[.]com and malwareaudit[.]com at DNS/proxy, and kill the zsh/curl process tree. Treat all local secrets as compromised. 3) HUNT: On the host look for ~/.local/.mpwd, /tmp/osalogging.zip, LaunchAgents at ~/.local/com.apple.<hex>.hcpi.plist, and outbound to 85.206.161[.]241:8443; sweep other Macs for the same domains and Terminal-spawned curl|zsh.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("curl", "zsh", "sh", "bash")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("agenticsora.com", "malwareaudit.com")
    or (ProcessCommandLine has "curl" and ProcessCommandLine has "base64 -D" and ProcessCommandLine has "zsh")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

DeviceProcessEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)

| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine

MacSync server-side AppleScript stealer: osascript, dscl authonly, keychain, ditto to /tmp/osalogging.zip AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts MacSync's stage-3 credential harvest: a server-side AppleScript pulled via curl '.../dynamic?txd=<token>' and run through osascript, password validation with 'dscl . authonly', Keychain Safe Storage extraction, and staging to /tmp/osalogging.zip via 'ditto -c -k'. Article-specific because it pins on the named staging archive, the authonly validation, and the osascript-from-curl chain. Rationale: Anchors on three verbatim MacSync artifacts from Huntress — the '.../dynamic?txd=' AppleScript fetch piped to osascript, 'dscl . authonly' password validation, and the '/tmp/osalogging.zip' ditto archive — none of which are typical of benign macOS admin activity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/macsync-stealer-rat-reverse-engineering • https://www.itsecurityguru.org/2026/07/30/fake-claude-install-guide-delivers-six-stage-macos-stealer-and-rat-huntress-finds/
ATT&CKT1059.002 T1555.001 T1560.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate MDM/admin scripts calling 'dscl . authonly' to validate a local password (rare and usually not paired with curl-fed osascript)
  • Backup or migration tooling using 'ditto -c -k' to archive folders (won't target /tmp/osalogging.zip)
  • Developer running an internal AppleScript via osascript (no 'dynamic?txd=' curl source)
  • Security product self-tests exercising Keychain access
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the osascript parent was a curl fetch to an attacker /dynamic endpoint; check whether /tmp/osalogging.zip, ~/.local/.mpwd, or /tmp/sync<rand>/ exist and were exfiltrated. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the Mac; rotate every credential class the stealer touches — macOS login/Keychain, browser-stored passwords, SSH keys, cloud/Kubernetes tokens, Telegram sessions. 3) HUNT: Look for the RAT LaunchAgent (~/.local/com.apple.<hex>.hcpi.plist) and C2 to 85.206.161[.]241:8443, and sweep the fleet for osascript spawned by curl and for 'dscl . authonly' invocations.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName =~ "osascript" and (ProcessCommandLine has "dynamic?txd=" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "curl"))
    or (FileName =~ "dscl" and ProcessCommandLine has "authonly")
    or (FileName =~ "ditto" and ProcessCommandLine has "osalogging.zip")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.

// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)

    or (FileName =~ "dscl" and ProcessCommandLine has "authonly")
    or (FileName =~ "ditto" and ProcessCommandLine has "osalogging.zip")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

MacSync RAT C2 / wallet-exfil to 85.206.161.241 and agenticsora/malwareaudit infrastructure AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound connections to MacSync's confirmed infrastructure: the Mach-O RAT C2 at 85.206.161[.]241:8443 (TLS/WebSocket) and the delivery/exfil domains agenticsora[.]com, malwareaudit[.]com, main.sdhomeinspectors[.]com, main.southcarolinacounselor[.]com. Article-specific because it uses the exact IP and domains corroborated in the Huntress reversing. Rationale: Uses the verbatim RAT C2 IP 85.206.161[.]241:8443 and the seed-phrase exfil domains (main.sdhomeinspectors[.]com, main.southcarolinacounselor[.]com) from the Huntress analysis, all present in the article's pre-extracted IOC set — direct atomic indicators with near-zero benign overlap. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/macsync-stealer-rat-reverse-engineering • https://cybersecuritynews.com/fake-claude-code-install-guide/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel or sandbox infrastructure in the org intentionally beaconing to the IOC for validation
  • A domain being sinkholed/reassigned to a benign parking host after takedown (verify current resolution)
  • Proxy/EDR log replay or backfill re-surfacing historical detonation traffic
  • Vulnerability scanners probing the exfil domains as part of an IOC-coverage test
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the InitiatingProcess making the connection (expect the MacSync Mach-O RAT under ~/.local); confirm bytes-out to 85.206.161[.]241:8443 and any POSTs to the /modules/wallets exfil paths. 2) CONTAIN: Block the IP and all four domains at egress, isolate the host, and remove the RAT LaunchAgent persistence. 3) HUNT: Reverse-search the fleet for any host that resolved or connected to these indicators, and for the stage-1 curl|zsh delivery and /tmp/osalogging.zip staging on those hosts.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "85.206.161.241"
    or RemoteUrl has_any ("agenticsora.com", "malwareaudit.com", "main.sdhomeinspectors.com", "main.southcarolinacounselor.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "85.206.161.241"
    or Url has_any ("agenticsora.com", "malwareaudit.com", "main.sdhomeinspectors.com", "main.southcarolinacounselor.com")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

MacSync wallet trojanization: app.asar swap + ad-hoc codesign of Ledger/Trezor apps AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts MacSync's stage-6 wallet tampering where installed wallet apps (Ledger Wallet/Live, Trezor Suite) are rewritten in place by swapping app.asar, injecting recovery-step-*.html phishing pages, and ad-hoc re-signing with 'codesign -f -s -'. Article-specific because it keys on modification of app.asar inside wallet bundles and the injected phishing filename pattern. Rationale: Targets the specific stage-6 artifacts Huntress documented — in-place app.asar replacement inside Ledger/Trezor bundles and injected 'recovery-step-*.html' seed-phrase phishing pages — a high-signal tamper pattern; medium FP because legitimate Electron wallet updates also rewrite app.asar, mitigated by the recovery-step filename and by pivoting on the writing process. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/macsync-stealer-rat-reverse-engineering • https://gbhackers.com/fake-claude-code-installer-3/
ATT&CKT1554 T1657
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Ledger Live / Trezor Suite auto-update rewriting its own app.asar (excluded when the writer is not the official updater or when recovery-step-* pages appear)
  • A developer rebuilding an Electron wallet app locally
  • MDM-pushed wallet app reinstall
  • Backup software restoring a wallet app bundle
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("Ledger Live", "Trezor Suite", "Squirrel", "com.apple.installer") and FileName !startswith "recovery-step-")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the process that wrote app.asar / recovery-step-* — if it is not the vendor's signed updater, treat as malicious; check for a preceding 'codesign -f -s -' ad-hoc re-sign of the wallet bundle. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, quarantine the tampered wallet app, and warn the user NOT to enter seed phrases; assume any wallet accessed post-tamper is compromised and initiate fund migration to a clean wallet. 3) HUNT: Sweep for the injected recovery-step-* pages and POSTs to main.sdhomeinspectors[.]com / main.southcarolinacounselor[.]com /modules/wallets, plus the upstream curl|zsh MacSync delivery on the same host.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileModified", "FileCreated")
| where (FileName =~ "app.asar" and FolderPath has_any ("Ledger", "Trezor"))
    or FileName startswith "recovery-step-"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceFileEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileModified", "FileCreated")
| where (FileName =~ "app.asar" and FolderPath has_any ("Ledger", "Trezor"))
    or FileName startswith "recovery-step-"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host

    category: process_creation

status: experimental

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("3db8befc08dc02ab7a76b5193abd81653775e8f3ceac5864c7c2188b2dbd3c54", "3ae26ed89d3a1a140edc89ca78513aba2895789ed0d0f64cad6605b6f2347c7e", "78dea0693ac2d70bdf8be7588667a75910e43fd84397ad484e710e37369a30f7", "9c09c303fa058c2d3e179969bd58ca5523775ff2d310fb2f8266ac74cb21ee81", "071bd109208eb1080ef525b5be394244cec467c59ffef5b8782cfb5e4850401d", "31566a1df7070f30cb990aa5eab310c1d4e0266c8776e9438138e5438ec1cff8", "230dff4bf9442a951dcd6898b2110924969a20668c20a43e3ceed6fcef65963e") or SHA1 in~ ("3db8befc08dc02ab7a76b5193abd81653775e8f3ceac5864c7c2188b2dbd3c54", "3ae26ed89d3a1a140edc89ca78513aba2895789ed0d0f64cad6605b6f2347c7e", "78dea0693ac2d70bdf8be7588667a75910e43fd84397ad484e710e37369a30f7", "9c09c303fa058c2d3e179969bd58ca5523775ff2d310fb2f8266ac74cb21ee81", "071bd109208eb1080ef525b5be394244cec467c59ffef5b8782cfb5e4850401d", "31566a1df7070f30cb990aa5eab310c1d4e0266c8776e9438138e5438ec1cff8", "230dff4bf9442a951dcd6898b2110924969a20668c20a43e3ceed6fcef65963e") or MD5 in~ ("3db8befc08dc02ab7a76b5193abd81653775e8f3ceac5864c7c2188b2dbd3c54", "3ae26ed89d3a1a140edc89ca78513aba2895789ed0d0f64cad6605b6f2347c7e", "78dea0693ac2d70bdf8be7588667a75910e43fd84397ad484e710e37369a30f7", "9c09c303fa058c2d3e179969bd58ca5523775ff2d310fb2f8266ac74cb21ee81", "071bd109208eb1080ef525b5be394244cec467c59ffef5b8782cfb5e4850401d", "31566a1df7070f30cb990aa5eab310c1d4e0266c8776e9438138e5438ec1cff8", "230dff4bf9442a951dcd6898b2110924969a20668c20a43e3ceed6fcef65963e")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("3db8befc08dc02ab7a76b5193abd81653775e8f3ceac5864c7c2188b2dbd3c54", "3ae26ed89d3a1a140edc89ca78513aba2895789ed0d0f64cad6605b6f2347c7e", "78dea0693ac2d70bdf8be7588667a75910e43fd84397ad484e710e37369a30f7", "9c09c303fa058c2d3e179969bd58ca5523775ff2d310fb2f8266ac74cb21ee81", "071bd109208eb1080ef525b5be394244cec467c59ffef5b8782cfb5e4850401d", "31566a1df7070f30cb990aa5eab310c1d4e0266c8776e9438138e5438ec1cff8", "230dff4bf9442a951dcd6898b2110924969a20668c20a43e3ceed6fcef65963e") or SHA1 in~ ("3db8befc08dc02ab7a76b5193abd81653775e8f3ceac5864c7c2188b2dbd3c54", "3ae26ed89d3a1a140edc89ca78513aba2895789ed0d0f64cad6605b6f2347c7e", "78dea0693ac2d70bdf8be7588667a75910e43fd84397ad484e710e37369a30f7", "9c09c303fa058c2d3e179969bd58ca5523775ff2d310fb2f8266ac74cb21ee81", "071bd109208eb1080ef525b5be394244cec467c59ffef5b8782cfb5e4850401d", "31566a1df7070f30cb990aa5eab310c1d4e0266c8776e9438138e5438ec1cff8", "230dff4bf9442a951dcd6898b2110924969a20668c20a43e3ceed6fcef65963e") or MD5 in~ ("3db8befc08dc02ab7a76b5193abd81653775e8f3ceac5864c7c2188b2dbd3c54", "3ae26ed89d3a1a140edc89ca78513aba2895789ed0d0f64cad6605b6f2347c7e", "78dea0693ac2d70bdf8be7588667a75910e43fd84397ad484e710e37369a30f7", "9c09c303fa058c2d3e179969bd58ca5523775ff2d310fb2f8266ac74cb21ee81", "071bd109208eb1080ef525b5be394244cec467c59ffef5b8782cfb5e4850401d", "31566a1df7070f30cb990aa5eab310c1d4e0266c8776e9438138e5438ec1cff8", "230dff4bf9442a951dcd6898b2110924969a20668c20a43e3ceed6fcef65963e")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["3db8befc08dc02ab7a76b5193abd81653775e8f3ceac5864c7c2188b2dbd3c54", "3ae26ed89d3a1a140edc89ca78513aba2895789ed0d0f64cad6605b6f2347c7e", "78dea0693ac2d70bdf8be7588667a75910e43fd84397ad484e710e37369a30f7", "9c09c303fa058c2d3e179969bd58ca5523775ff2d310fb2f8266ac74cb21ee81", "071bd109208eb1080ef525b5be394244cec467c59ffef5b8782cfb5e4850401d", "31566a1df7070f30cb990aa5eab310c1d4e0266c8776e9438138e5438ec1cff8", "230dff4bf9442a951dcd6898b2110924969a20668c20a43e3ceed6fcef65963e"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Article-specific behavioural hunt — You were onto something with “It’s the Climb,” Miley
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Zoho Assist Unattended Agent deployment (Warlock / Storm-2603 ransomware) · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Trojanized MeshAgent running outside its install path (Sinobi ransomware C2) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Email-hiding inbox rules created post-compromise (BEC / mailbox concealment) · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Successful Entra ID device-code authentication (ARToken/EvilTokens PhaaS MFA bypass) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts successful OAuth device-code grant sign-ins in Entra ID, the flow abused by the ARToken/EvilTokens phishing-as-a-service platform to bypass MFA and mint persistent refresh tokens. Device-code auth is rare/unused in most tenants, so any success warrants review for account takeover. Rationale: Grounds on the ARToken/EvilTokens device-code phishing pattern named in the corroborated Talos IR Q2 2026 report; device-code auth success is inherently rare and high-signal for token-theft AiTM. Cross-checked https://blog.talosintelligence.com/ir-trends-q2-2026/. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/ir-trends-q2-2026/
ATT&CKT1621 T1528 T1566.002
Data sourcesAuthentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate device-code sign-in from IoT/kiosk/CLI tooling (Azure CLI 'az login --use-device-code')
  • Conference-room / smart-TV Teams device provisioning
  • Developers using device-code flow for headless service auth
  • PowerShell modules (Microsoft.Graph, Az) prompting device-code login on servers
Suppression filter
| where ClientAppUsed !in ("Mobile Apps and Desktop clients") or Application !has_any ("Microsoft Azure CLI","Microsoft Azure PowerShell","Microsoft Graph Command Line Tools")
Response runbook
1) Triage: For each hit, confirm whether the user legitimately performs device-code logins; check the IP/geo/ASN and UserAgent against the user's baseline and look for impossible travel. 2) Contain: If unrecognized, revoke sessions/refresh tokens (Revoke-MgUserSignInSession), force password reset, and re-register MFA; block the source IP. 3) Hunt: Pivot on the AccountUpn for subsequent non-interactive token use, new inbox rules, OAuth app consents, and mailbox/SharePoint access from the same IP.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AuthenticationProcessingDetails has "Device Code"
| where ErrorCode == 0            // successful device-code grant
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, Application, ApplicationId, IPAddress, Country, City, UserAgent, ClientAppUsed
| order by Timestamp desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where AuthenticationProcessingDetails has "Device Code"
| where ResultType == 0           // successful device-code grant
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName, AppId, IPAddress, Location, UserAgent, ClientAppUsed
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Trojanized MeshAgent running outside its install path (Sinobi ransomware C2) AICommand & Control High
Hunts MeshAgent / MeshCentral processes executing from non-standard locations, the trojanized SYSTEM-level auto-start C2 used by Sinobi ransomware operators. Legitimate MeshCentral installs live under a fixed program path; execution elsewhere indicates an attacker-deployed agent. Rationale: Uses the corroborated report detail that Sinobi deployed a trojanized MeshAgent as SYSTEM auto-start C2; anchoring on the MeshAgent binary/product plus a path-exclusion turns a legit tool into a high-fidelity attacker signal. Cross-checked Talos IR Q2 2026 and detection.fyi renamed-MeshAgent Sigma. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/ir-trends-q2-2026/ • https://detection.fyi/sigmahq/sigma/macos/process_creation/proc_creation_macos_remote_access_tools_renamed_meshagent_execution/
ATT&CKT1219 T1543.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sanctioned MeshCentral deployment installed to a custom directory by IT
  • Portable MeshAgent run from a technician's USB during legitimate support
  • Security-team red-team or RMM evaluation testing
  • MSP-managed endpoints where MeshCentral is the approved RMM
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("approved-rmm-svc") and SHA256 !in ("<known-good-meshagent-sha256-from-your-approved-build>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: Verify whether MeshCentral is an approved RMM for this host/business unit; inspect the file path, SHA256 (reputation), signer, and the parent process that dropped it. 2) Contain: If unsanctioned, isolate the host, kill the MeshAgent service/process, and block its outbound WSS destination at the proxy/firewall. 3) Hunt: Search other hosts for the same SHA256/service, look for co-located ransomware staging (rclone.exe, GPO logon scripts, .SINOBI files) and enumerate the account that installed the service.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName has "meshagent"
    or ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName has "MeshAgent"
    or ProcessVersionInfoProductName has "MeshCentral"
| where not(FolderPath has_any (@"\Program Files\Mesh Agent\", @"\Program Files (x86)\Mesh Agent\"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, ProcessIntegrityLevel, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has "meshagent"
| where NewProcessName !has @"\Program Files\Mesh Agent\"
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, TokenElevationType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Zoho Assist Unattended Agent deployment (Warlock / Storm-2603 ransomware) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts execution of Zoho Assist Unattended Agent binaries, the RMM tool Warlock (Storm-2603) operators install for persistent, session-independent remote control ahead of encryption. Flags the agent/installer binaries especially when run non-interactively or as SYSTEM. Rationale: Anchors on the corroborated report detail that Warlock/Storm-2603 deployed the Zoho Assist Unattended Agent for persistence; the unattended/SYSTEM context distinguishes attacker deployment from interactive helpdesk use. Cross-checked Talos IR Q2 2026 and Intel471 RMM-abuse writeup. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/ir-trends-q2-2026/ • https://www.intel471.com/blog/understanding-and-threat-hunting-for-rmm-software-misuse
ATT&CKT1219 T1543.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sanctioned Zoho Assist use by an internal or outsourced IT helpdesk
  • MSP performing legitimate unattended-access provisioning
  • Software inventory/patching workflows that bundle Zoho
  • User-initiated Zoho support session for a real ticket
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("helpdesk-svc","msp-support") and DeviceName !in~ ("<known-helpdesk-hosts>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: Confirm whether Zoho Assist is an approved support tool for this host; check who initiated it, the parent process, and whether an unattended (session-independent) install was performed. 2) Contain: If unauthorized, isolate the host, remove the Zoho Assist Unattended service, and block Zoho Assist gateway domains for the affected segment. 3) Hunt: Enumerate other hosts with the same binary/service, review for follow-on ransomware TTPs (rclone staging, shadow-copy deletion, GPO logon scripts) and audit the service account used for install.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has "ZOHO"
    or ProcessVersionInfoProductName has "Zoho Assist"
    or FileName in~ ("ZA_Access.exe","ZA_Connect.exe","ZMAgent.exe")
    or ProcessCommandLine has "Zoho_Assist"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("unattended","install","silent") or ProcessIntegrityLevel == "System"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, ProcessIntegrityLevel, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("ZA_Access.exe","ZA_Connect.exe","ZMAgent.exe","Zoho_Assist")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, TokenElevationType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Email-hiding inbox rules created post-compromise (BEC / mailbox concealment) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts creation/modification of Exchange Online inbox rules that delete, mark-as-read, redirect, or move messages to hidden folders — the concealment step Talos IR observed after auth-abuse account takeover, often preceding large outbound email bursts. Distinct from generic phishing-click detections. Rationale: Grounds on the corroborated Talos IR finding of email-hiding rule creation (T1564.008) and outbound-email spikes after auth abuse; scoping to delete/redirect/mark-read parameters keeps only concealment-intent rules rather than benign filing rules. Cross-checked Talos IR Q2 2026. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/ir-trends-q2-2026/
ATT&CKT1564.008 T1114.003
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User legitimately auto-filing newsletters into folders or Deleted Items
  • Executive assistant configuring forwarding to a shared mailbox
  • Mailbox migration/cleanup tooling that rewrites rules in bulk
  • Out-of-office or VIP triage rules marking mail as read
Suppression filter
| where not (Parameters has "MoveToFolder" and Parameters !has_any ("DeleteMessage","ForwardTo","RedirectTo","Deleted Items"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: Review the rule parameters and the creating IP/UserAgent against the user's baseline; check if the same session had a risky/device-code sign-in or impossible travel. 2) Contain: If malicious, remove the inbox rule, revoke sessions, reset credentials + re-register MFA, and search sent items for fraudulent/BEC messages. 3) Hunt: Correlate with outbound email volume spikes (e.g., thousands of messages), other users with identical rule patterns, and OAuth app consents from the same source IP.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Exchange Online"
| where ActionType in ("New-InboxRule","Set-InboxRule","UpdateInboxRules","Update-InboxRules")
| extend Raw = tostring(RawEventData)
| where Raw has_any ("DeleteMessage","Deleted Items","MarkAsRead","Junk Email","MoveToFolder","ForwardTo","RedirectTo")
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, IPAddress, ActionType, ObjectName, Raw
| order by Timestamp desc
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Operation in ("New-InboxRule","Set-InboxRule","UpdateInboxRules")
| where Parameters has_any ("DeleteMessage","Deleted Items","MarkAsRead","Junk Email","MoveToFolder","ForwardTo","RedirectTo")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, ClientIP, Operation, OfficeWorkload, Parameters
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),

| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")

| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT

| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject

    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count

    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")

SecurityEvent

| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,

| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that

references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"

// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "fc18d4060c6dad3057c0b5a70a2081473e066951720cafbd2aa159d3aaccf2e1", "90b1456cdbe6bc2779ea0b4736ed9a998a71ae37390331b6ba87e389a49d3d59", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "ded73d04bb3e3525226de64c38a332e3", "c2efb2dcacba6d3ccc175b6ce1b7ed0a"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
—
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time

Flyto2 flyto-verification unauthenticated POST /run on :8344 (CVE-2026-67426 SSRF entry) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts inbound HTTP POST to the /run endpoint of the flyto-verification service on TCP 8344 from non-loopback/remote sources. The shipped Dockerfile binds 0.0.0.0:8344 and /run has no auth dependency, so any remote POST /run is the unauthenticated entry point for the callback_url SSRF and runner-secret exfiltration chain. Rationale: Uses the article's concrete endpoint (POST /run) and the Dockerfile-shipped port 8344 (verification_service.py:363-364, Dockerfile.verification CMD). Restricting to external/remote sources leverages the fix guidance ('bind loopback by default') to separate attack traffic from legit internal callers. Corroborated against the GitLab advisory confirming the 0.0.0.0:8344 exposure. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/flyto-core/CVE-2026-67426/ • https://cvereports.com/reports/CVE-2026-67426
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate internal verification jobs POSTing /run from an app tier reachable via a public NAT egress IP
  • Vulnerability scanners / ASM tools probing the /run path on 8344
  • Load-balancer or uptime health checks hitting /run
  • Developer testing the verification service from a bastion/VPN with a public source IP
Suppression filter
| where not(SourceIP in ("<known-healthcheck-ip>"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the source IP is external and not an expected internal caller; pull the full request (body should contain callback_url/workflowYaml) from app or proxy logs and check whether the host is running flyto-core <= 2.26.6. 2) Contain: rebind flyto-verification to loopback (or firewall 8344 to internal only), and rotate FLYTO_RUNNER_SECRET immediately since it may already be exfiltrated. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC2/UC3 — search for outbound connections from the verification host to 169.254.169.254 or to any public IP, and audit engine-callback authentications using the (now-possibly-leaked) runner secret.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where LocalPort == 8344
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, LocalPort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DestinationPort == 8344
| where RequestMethod == "POST"
| where RequestURL has "/run"
| where isnotempty(SourceIP) and not(SourceIP startswith "10." or SourceIP startswith "192.168." or SourceIP startswith "172.16." or SourceIP startswith "127.")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

flyto-verification SSRF to cloud metadata IP (169.254.169.254) — runner-secret/IMDS theft AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts outbound connections from the flyto-verification runner (python/uvicorn/gunicorn/flyto-verification) to cloud instance-metadata endpoints (169.254.169.254, 100.100.100.200, metadata.google.internal). CVE-2026-67426's callback_url bypasses the target_allowed allowlist and SSRF guard, letting an attacker force the service to POST to the IMDS with a controlled body and harvest instance credentials. Rationale: The article explicitly names 'cloud-metadata IP' as an SSRF target; MITRE T1552.005 and Elastic's prebuilt IMDS-SSRF rule confirm 169.254.169.254 (plus Alibaba 100.100.100.200 / GCP metadata.google.internal) as the canonical endpoints. Scoping to the python/flyto-verification process removes legit cloud-agent IMDS calls, making a web-runner->IMDS connection a near-zero-FP signal. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/005/ • https://www.elastic.co/docs/reference/security/prebuilt-rules/rules/cross-platform/credential_access_web_server_cloud_imds_ssrf_request • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/flyto-core/CVE-2026-67426/
ATT&CKT1552.005 T1190
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate flyto workflow that intentionally targets an internal 169.254.x host as a callback (rare/misconfig)
  • Cloud SDK embedded in the same python venv making a genuine IMDSv2 token call for the app's own role
  • Security testing / red-team validation of the SSRF fix
  • Sidecar or observability agent sharing the process name 'python' reaching metadata for instance tags
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("flyto", "verification")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating process is the flyto-verification runner and capture the destination path/body; check IMDS access logs (if IMDSv2 enabled) for a token issuance from this host at the same time. 2) Contain: rotate FLYTO_RUNNER_SECRET and any instance-role credentials that IMDS could have returned; enforce IMDSv2 (HttpTokens=required) and block 169.254.0.0/16 egress from the container; upgrade flyto-core to 2.26.7. 3) Hunt: search CloudTrail/AAD/GCP audit for use of the instance-role or managed-identity credentials from unexpected IPs shortly after this event, and check UC3 for the secret being POSTed to an external attacker host.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("169.254.169.254", "100.100.100.200") or RemoteUrl has "metadata.google.internal"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python", "python3", "uvicorn", "gunicorn", "flyto-verification", "flyto")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession

| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, Url
| order by TimeGenerated desc

flyto-verification runner egress to external public host — FLYTO_RUNNER_SECRET exfiltration AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the flyto-verification/python runner initiating outbound connections to public (non-RFC1918, non-link-local) destinations. Because callback_url is attacker-controlled and the service unconditionally attaches X-Internal-Key: $FLYTO_RUNNER_SECRET, any egress from this backend runner to an arbitrary internet host is a candidate secret-exfiltration callback. Rationale: Grounded in the sink from the advisory: post_callback -> session.post(callback_url, headers={'X-Internal-Key': FLYTO_RUNNER_SECRET}) (verification_service.py:330-335). A backend verification runner that is only supposed to call the internal engine should never egress to a public IP, so process-scoped public egress is a high-value exfiltration hunt for the leaked runner secret. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-jx74-cqjv-2c67 • https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-67428
ATT&CKT1567 T1552
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate engine callback endpoint hosted on a public IP / SaaS domain rather than internal
  • Python dependency/package fetches (pip, telemetry SDKs) from the same runner venv
  • Outbound calls to a public webhook/notification service used by real workflows
  • CDN or object-storage uploads the workflow performs as designed
Suppression filter
| where RemoteUrl !has "pypi.org" and RemoteUrl !has "pythonhosted.org"
Response runbook
1) Triage: resolve the public RemoteIP/RemoteUrl and compare against the documented internal engine callback host; if it is unknown/attacker-looking, capture the flow and any TLS SNI. 2) Contain: block egress from the flyto-verification container except to the known engine, rotate FLYTO_RUNNER_SECRET, and upgrade to flyto-core 2.26.7. 3) Hunt: correlate with UC1 (inbound POST /run carrying that callback_url) and UC2 (IMDS access), and review engine-callback auth logs for forged authenticated callbacks using the leaked X-Internal-Key.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where (InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("flyto-verification", "flyto")) or (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python", "python3", "uvicorn", "gunicorn") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "flyto")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where ActionType in ("ConnectionSuccess", "ConnectionAttempt")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), Count=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort, 10) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl
